Drift detection compares actual resource configurations with the stack template.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stack outputs: Outputs export values.
• Change sets: Change sets preview template updates.
• Termination protection: Termination protection prevents stack deletion.

Key takeaway: Find manual changes with drift detection.

stem: A team wants to protect a production database resource in a CloudFormation stack from being replaced or deleted during updates. What should they use?

choices.text: A change set created for each stack update
An output that exports the database endpoint
A parameter with a default database name
A stack policy denying updates to that resource

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Stack policies define which resources can be updated, protecting critical resources from unintended replacement or deletion.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A change set created for each stack update: Change sets preview but do not block.
• An output that exports the database endpoint: Outputs export values.
• A parameter with a default database name: Parameters provide inputs.

Key takeaway: Protect critical stack resources with stack policies (and DeletionPolicy).

stem: An operations team must apply OS patches to 500 EC2 instances monthly during a maintenance window. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector findings reviewed manually each month
CloudFormation stack updates for each instance's AMI
AWS Trusted Advisor checks refreshed every weekend
Systems Manager Patch Manager with a maintenance window

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Patch Manager automates patching with baselines and maintenance windows across fleets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Inspector findings reviewed manually…: Inspector finds vulnerabilities but does not patch.
• CloudFormation stack updates for each…: Stack updates are not a patching process.
• AWS Trusted Advisor checks refreshed every…: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.

Key takeaway: Fleet patching → Systems Manager Patch Manager.

stem: Engineers need shell access to private EC2 instances without opening inbound ports or managing SSH keys, with sessions logged. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A VPN to each instance's public IP
Systems Manager Session Manager
A bastion host with port 22 open
EC2 Instance Connect over the internet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Session Manager provides audited shell access through the SSM agent without inbound ports or SSH keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A VPN to each instance's public IP: VPNs to public IPs add complexity and exposure.
• A bastion host with port 22 open: Bastions require open ports and key management.
• EC2 Instance Connect over the internet: Instance Connect over the internet needs reachable SSH.

Key takeaway: Keyless, portless, audited access → Session Manager.

stem: A team wants to run the same shell command on 200 EC2 instances at once without logging in to each. Which feature fits?

choices.text: AWS Config custom rules
CloudFormation drift detection
Systems Manager Run Command
EC2 user data on next launch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Run Command executes commands across many managed instances at once, with output logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config custom rules: Config rules evaluate compliance.
• CloudFormation drift detection: Drift detection finds template differences.
• EC2 user data on next launch: User data runs at launch, not on demand.

Key takeaway: Ad hoc fleet commands → Run Command.

stem: A team wants to automate a multi-step operational procedure, such as creating an AMI, testing it, and updating a launch template. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Systems Manager Automation runbooks
CloudWatch Logs metric filters
Amazon S3 Event Notifications
IAM Access Analyzer findings

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automation runbooks define and run multi-step operational workflows across AWS resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch Logs metric filters: Metric filters create metrics from logs.
• Amazon S3 Event Notifications: S3 events trigger on object changes.
• IAM Access Analyzer findings: Access Analyzer reviews permissions.

Key takeaway: Multi-step operational procedures → SSM Automation.

stem: Applications need configuration values and secrets, such as database endpoints and passwords, managed centrally. Which TWO services fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront Functions
Systems Manager Parameter Store
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
AWS Direct Connect gateway
AWS Secrets Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parameter Store holds configuration (including SecureString values), and Secrets Manager stores secrets with rotation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon CloudFront Functions: CloudFront Functions run at the edge.
• Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive: Glacier Deep Archive is archival storage.
• AWS Direct Connect gateway: Direct Connect provides private connectivity.

Key takeaway: Config → Parameter Store; rotating secrets → Secrets Manager.

stem: A team uses Terraform for AWS infrastructure. Several engineers run it, and the state file occasionally becomes corrupted from concurrent runs. What should they configure?

choices.text: A local state file on each laptop
A separate AWS account per engineer
A shorter Terraform plan output
A remote backend with state locking

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A remote backend (such as S3 with locking) stores shared state and prevents concurrent modifications.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A local state file on each laptop: Local state causes conflicts and loss.
• A separate AWS account per engineer: Separate accounts do not fix shared-state conflicts.
• A shorter Terraform plan output: Plan output length is irrelevant.

Key takeaway: Shared Terraform state needs a remote backend with locking.

stem: A team wants EC2 instances launched by Auto Scaling to always use the latest approved, hardened AMI built monthly. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Manually rebuilding an AMI whenever someone remembers to
Asking developers to patch instances after they launch
EC2 Image Builder pipelines that update the launch template
Using the original AMI from two years ago for stability

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Image Builder automates building, testing, and distributing AMIs and can update launch templates with the new image.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manually rebuilding an AMI whenever someone…: Manual builds are unreliable.
• Asking developers to patch instances after…: Post-launch patching delays protection.
• Using the original AMI from two years ago…: Old AMIs lack patches.

Key takeaway: Automated golden AMIs → EC2 Image Builder.

stem: Which TWO Systems Manager capabilities help an operations team maintain fleet compliance? (Select TWO)

choices.text: State Manager to keep instances in a defined configuration
Session Manager to deploy CloudFormation stacks
Parameter Store to host static website files
Incident Manager to schedule quarterly staff meetings
Inventory to collect installed software and configuration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inventory shows what is installed, and State Manager enforces desired configurations over time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Session Manager to deploy CloudFormation stacks: Session Manager provides shell access.
• Parameter Store to host static website files: Parameter Store stores parameters, not websites.
• Incident Manager to schedule quarterly staff…: Incident Manager handles incident response, not meetings.

Key takeaway: Inventory shows state; State Manager enforces it.

stem: A CloudFormation template must create resources in a specific order: a VPC before subnets, and subnets before instances. How is this handled?

choices.text: Order cannot be controlled, so separate stacks are required for each tier
Resources are always created in the order they appear in the template
References such as Ref create dependencies, and DependsOn adds explicit order
The engineer must create each resource manually in the correct order

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation infers dependencies from references and uses DependsOn for explicit ordering when needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Order cannot be controlled, so separate…: Ordering is controllable within a stack.
• Resources are always created in the order…: Template order does not determine creation order.
• The engineer must create each resource…: Manual creation defeats IaC.

Key takeaway: Dependencies come from references and DependsOn.

stem: A team wants to be notified and take automated action whenever an Auto Scaling group fails to launch an instance. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A monthly review of Auto Scaling activity history logs
An EventBridge rule on Auto Scaling launch-failure events
A CloudFormation output listing the group's instances
An S3 lifecycle policy on the group's log bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Auto Scaling emits events for launch failures that EventBridge can route to SNS or Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A monthly review of Auto Scaling activity…: Monthly reviews are too slow.
• A CloudFormation output listing the group's…: Outputs do not detect failures.
• An S3 lifecycle policy on the group's log bucket: Lifecycle policies manage storage.

Key takeaway: React to Auto Scaling events with EventBridge.

stem: A team wants to reuse a standard, approved VPC design across many CloudFormation templates. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Nested stacks or modules for the VPC component
Create the VPC manually and document the steps
Copy and paste the VPC code into each template
Deploy one VPC and share its password with teams

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Nested stacks and CloudFormation modules package reusable, versioned components.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Create the VPC manually and document the steps: Manual creation defeats IaC.
• Copy and paste the VPC code into each template: Copy-paste leads to drift and inconsistency.
• Deploy one VPC and share its password with teams: VPCs are not shared by passwords.

Key takeaway: Reuse IaC components with nested stacks or modules.

stem: A company wants continuous threat detection for its accounts, such as compromised credentials or crypto-mining, with no agents to manage. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Macie
Amazon Inspector
AWS Artifact
Amazon GuardDuty

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs to detect threats without agents.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Macie: Macie finds sensitive data in S3.
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities.
• AWS Artifact: Artifact provides compliance documents.

Key takeaway: Account threat detection → GuardDuty.

stem: Security wants findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie across 30 accounts in one place with security standard checks. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Log in to each of the 30 accounts separately and review each console
Security Hub with a delegated administrator and cross-account aggregation
Disable the services in member accounts to reduce total finding noise
Export findings manually to spreadsheets and email them each week

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security Hub aggregates findings across accounts and Regions and runs security standard checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Log in to each of the 30 accounts separately…: Per-account review does not scale.
• Disable the services in member accounts to…: Disabling services removes protection.
• Export findings manually to spreadsheets and…: Manual exports are slow and error-prone.

Key takeaway: Centralize security findings with Security Hub.

stem: A company must prevent member accounts from disabling CloudTrail, even with administrator permissions. Which control fits?

choices.text: A service control policy that denies StopLogging and DeleteTrail
A tag on the trail indicating it must never be disabled by anyone
An IAM policy attached to the developers group in each account
A CloudWatch alarm that notifies security when a trail stops logging

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs set maximum permissions for member accounts, so denied actions cannot be performed even by administrators.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A tag on the trail indicating it must never…: Tags do not enforce anything.
• An IAM policy attached to the developers…: Account administrators could change IAM policies.
• A CloudWatch alarm that notifies security…: Alarms detect but do not prevent.

Key takeaway: Preventive guardrails across accounts → SCPs.

stem: A team needs to find IAM roles and S3 buckets that are shared with principals outside the organization. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Detective
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Cost Explorer
IAM Access Analyzer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Access Analyzer identifies resources shared with external principals, using the organization as the zone of trust.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Detective: Detective investigates security findings.
• AWS Trusted Advisor: Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks.
• AWS Cost Explorer: Cost Explorer analyzes spending.

Key takeaway: Find external access → IAM Access Analyzer.

stem: A company must continuously evaluate its resources against a set of compliance rules and deploy the same rules across all accounts. Which feature fits?

choices.text: CloudFormation drift detection run manually every quarter
CloudWatch dashboards showing resource counts per account
AWS Config conformance packs deployed across the organization
Trusted Advisor checks reviewed by each account's owner

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Conformance packs bundle Config rules and remediation and can be deployed organization-wide.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFormation drift detection run manually…: Drift detection covers stack templates only and is manual here.
• CloudWatch dashboards showing resource…: Counts do not evaluate compliance.
• Trusted Advisor checks reviewed by each…: Trusted Advisor is not a compliance framework.

Key takeaway: Organization-wide compliance rules → Config conformance packs.

stem: All new EBS volumes in an account must be encrypted automatically. What is the simplest control?

choices.text: Take encrypted snapshots of volumes every night
Ask engineers to select encryption for each volume
Use only instance store volumes for all instances
Enable EBS encryption by default in each Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS encryption by default ensures every new volume is encrypted in that Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Take encrypted snapshots of volumes every night: Snapshots do not encrypt existing volumes in place.
• Ask engineers to select encryption for each…: Manual selection is error-prone.
• Use only instance store volumes for all…: Instance store is not persistent storage.

Key takeaway: Enforce EBS encryption with encryption by default.

stem: An existing unencrypted RDS instance must be encrypted. What is the correct approach?

choices.text: Snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption, and restore a new instance
Enable encryption directly on the running instance in the console
Create an encrypted read replica and promote it without any snapshot
Modify the instance class, which encrypts storage automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Encryption cannot be enabled on an existing unencrypted instance; copying a snapshot with encryption and restoring creates an encrypted instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable encryption directly on the running…: Encryption cannot be turned on in place.
• Create an encrypted read replica and promote…: Read replicas of unencrypted instances cannot be encrypted.
• Modify the instance class, which encrypts…: Instance class changes do not encrypt storage.

Key takeaway: Encrypt existing RDS via encrypted snapshot copy and restore.

stem: A company wants all S3 buckets in its account to reject public access, regardless of individual bucket policies. Which setting fits?

choices.text: S3 Object Lock in governance mode per bucket
S3 Block Public Access at the account level
S3 Transfer Acceleration for all buckets
S3 Versioning on every existing bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Account-level Block Public Access overrides bucket settings that would allow public access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Object Lock in governance mode per bucket: Object Lock prevents deletion, not public access.
• S3 Transfer Acceleration for all buckets: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads.
• S3 Versioning on every existing bucket: Versioning keeps old versions.

Key takeaway: Prevent public buckets account-wide with Block Public Access.

stem: A company must rotate a database password automatically every 30 days without application downtime. Which service fits?

choices.text: A password in an S3 text file
Parameter Store standard String
AWS Secrets Manager with rotation
A password in EC2 user data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager rotates secrets on a schedule with built-in support for RDS databases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A password in an S3 text file: S3 text files are not secure secret storage.
• Parameter Store standard String: A standard String parameter has no rotation.
• A password in EC2 user data: User data is not a secret store.

Key takeaway: Automatic secret rotation → Secrets Manager.

stem: A public website on an ALB needs protection from SQL injection and bad bots. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS WAF with managed rule groups on the ALB
A network ACL with an explicit allow rule only
A security group allowing traffic from all IPs
AWS Shield Standard with no other controls

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks attacks such as SQL injection using managed rule groups, including bot control.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A network ACL with an explicit allow rule only: NACLs filter by IP and port.
• A security group allowing traffic from all IPs: Security groups filter by port and source, not request content.
• AWS Shield Standard with no other controls: Shield Standard protects against network DDoS, not SQL injection.

Key takeaway: Layer 7 web attacks → AWS WAF.

stem: Which TWO actions protect data in transit to an ALB-hosted application? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enable S3 versioning on the log bucket
Allow only port 80 in the security group
Store the TLS private key in user data
Use an HTTPS listener with an ACM certificate
Redirect HTTP requests to HTTPS on the listener

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An HTTPS listener with an ACM certificate encrypts traffic, and redirecting HTTP to HTTPS enforces it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable S3 versioning on the log bucket: Versioning protects objects, not transit.
• Allow only port 80 in the security group: Port 80 alone is unencrypted.
• Store the TLS private key in user data: Private keys must not be in user data.

Key takeaway: Enforce TLS at the load balancer.

stem: A company needs to ensure that EC2 instances can only be launched with approved AMIs and required tags. Which TWO controls help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A shared administrator password for all engineers
A dashboard that shows instance counts by Region
Config rules that detect non-approved AMIs and missing tags
Disabling CloudTrail to reduce the volume of logs
IAM policies with conditions on AMI IDs and request tags

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM conditions prevent non-compliant launches, and Config rules detect any that slip through.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A shared administrator password for all…: Shared passwords weaken accountability.
• A dashboard that shows instance counts by Region: Counts do not enforce anything.
• Disabling CloudTrail to reduce the volume of…: Disabling CloudTrail removes auditing.

Key takeaway: Combine preventive IAM conditions with detective Config rules.

stem: A company must find sensitive data such as credit card numbers stored in S3 across many buckets. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Macie
AWS Resource Access Manager
AWS Firewall Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon GuardDuty: GuardDuty detects threats.
• AWS Resource Access Manager: RAM shares resources.
• AWS Firewall Manager: Firewall Manager manages firewall rules across accounts.

Key takeaway: Sensitive data discovery in S3 → Macie.

stem: Instances in a private subnet need to download updates from the internet but must not accept inbound connections. What is required?

choices.text: An internet gateway attached directly to the private subnet
An S3 gateway endpoint in the private subnet's route table
A VPC peering connection to another account's public VPC
A NAT gateway in a public subnet and a private route to it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway in a public subnet lets private instances initiate outbound connections while blocking inbound ones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An internet gateway attached directly to the…: Internet gateways attach to VPCs, and a route to one makes the subnet public.
• An S3 gateway endpoint in the private…: Gateway endpoints only reach S3 or DynamoDB.
• A VPC peering connection to another…: Peering does not provide internet access.

Key takeaway: Private outbound internet → NAT gateway in a public subnet.

stem: A company must connect 30 VPCs and an on-premises network with centralized routing. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Transit Gateway
An internet gateway per VPC
A NAT gateway in each VPC
VPC peering in a full mesh

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway acts as a hub for VPCs and on-premises connections, avoiding a complex peering mesh.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An internet gateway per VPC: Internet gateways do not connect VPCs.
• A NAT gateway in each VPC: NAT gateways provide outbound internet access.
• VPC peering in a full mesh: A full mesh of 30 VPCs is hard to manage and peering is non-transitive.

Key takeaway: Many VPCs plus on-premises → Transit Gateway hub.

stem: Private EC2 instances access S3 heavily through a NAT gateway, and data processing charges are high. Which change reduces cost?

choices.text: Add a second NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone
Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint to the private route tables
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket
Move the instances to a public subnet with public IP addresses

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints route S3 traffic privately with no NAT data processing charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Add a second NAT gateway in the same…: More NAT gateways add cost.
• Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the…: Transfer Acceleration adds cost and targets long-distance uploads.
• Move the instances to a public subnet with…: Public subnets expose instances unnecessarily.

Key takeaway: S3 from private subnets → gateway endpoint instead of NAT.

stem: Applications in a VPC must call Amazon SQS privately without internet access. Which option fits?

choices.text: An egress-only internet gateway
A Direct Connect public VIF only
An interface VPC endpoint for SQS
A gateway VPC endpoint for SQS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) provide private access to services such as SQS; gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An egress-only internet gateway: Egress-only gateways are for IPv6 internet traffic.
• A Direct Connect public VIF only: A public VIF reaches public endpoints over Direct Connect, not privately from the VPC.
• A gateway VPC endpoint for SQS: Gateway endpoints support only S3 and DynamoDB.

Key takeaway: Private access to most AWS services → interface endpoints.

stem: A global audience experiences slow downloads of static assets from an S3 bucket in one Region. Which service improves performance?

choices.text: Route 53 simple routing to the bucket
A larger EC2 instance in front of S3
Amazon CloudFront with the bucket as origin
S3 Cross-Region Replication to one Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches content at edge locations close to users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 simple routing to the bucket: DNS routing alone does not cache content.
• A larger EC2 instance in front of S3: An instance adds a bottleneck.
• S3 Cross-Region Replication to one Region: Replicating to one more Region still leaves many users far away.

Key takeaway: Global static content → CloudFront.

stem: After updating files in the S3 origin, users still see old content through CloudFront. The team needs the change visible now. What should they do?

choices.text: Increase the default TTL on the cache behavior
Disable CloudFront logging for the distribution
Delete and recreate the S3 bucket with the same name
Create a CloudFront invalidation for the changed paths

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Invalidations remove cached objects from edge locations so the next request fetches the new version.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the default TTL on the cache behavior: A longer TTL keeps old content longer.
• Disable CloudFront logging for the distribution: Logging does not affect caching.
• Delete and recreate the S3 bucket with the…: Recreating the bucket is disruptive and unnecessary.

Key takeaway: Refresh cached content with invalidations or versioned names.

stem: A company wants to route users to the AWS Region that gives them the lowest latency. Which Route 53 routing policy fits?

choices.text: Latency-based routing
Multivalue routing
Simple routing
Weighted routing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Latency-based routing answers with the Region that offers the lowest latency for the user.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multivalue routing: Multivalue returns several healthy records.
• Simple routing: Simple returns one record set.
• Weighted routing: Weighted splits by percentages.

Key takeaway: Lowest latency Region → latency-based routing.

stem: A company needs the zone apex, example.com, to point to an Application Load Balancer. Which record type fits?

choices.text: An MX record for the ALB
A Route 53 alias record
A TXT record with the IP
A CNAME record at the apex

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Alias records can point the zone apex to AWS resources such as ALBs; CNAMEs are not allowed at the apex.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An MX record for the ALB: MX records are for mail.
• A TXT record with the IP: TXT records hold text and do not route traffic.
• A CNAME record at the apex: CNAMEs cannot be used at the zone apex.

Key takeaway: Apex to AWS resources → alias records.

stem: A company wants S3 content served only through CloudFront, blocking direct access to the bucket. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Origin access control plus a bucket policy allowing only the distribution
Public read on the bucket with CloudFront logging turned on
S3 Transfer Acceleration enabled on the bucket's endpoint
A security group on the bucket that allows CloudFront IPs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OAC lets CloudFront sign requests to S3, and the bucket policy allows only that distribution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public read on the bucket with CloudFront…: Public read allows direct access.
• S3 Transfer Acceleration enabled on the…: Transfer Acceleration does not restrict access.
• A security group on the bucket that allows…: S3 buckets do not use security groups.

Key takeaway: Restrict S3 to CloudFront with OAC and a bucket policy.

stem: An instance in a public subnet cannot be reached on port 443. The security group allows 443 inbound. What should be checked next?

choices.text: The CloudTrail trail configuration for the Region where the instance runs
The instance's IAM role permissions for Amazon S3 buckets in the account
The subnet's network ACL rules for inbound 443 and outbound ephemeral ports
The S3 bucket policy for the application's static files and assets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs are stateless; they must allow inbound 443 and outbound ephemeral ports for responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The CloudTrail trail configuration for the…: CloudTrail does not affect traffic.
• The instance's IAM role permissions for…: IAM roles do not affect network reachability.
• The S3 bucket policy for the application's…: Bucket policies do not affect instance access.

Key takeaway: Check NACLs (stateless) when security groups look correct.

stem: An engineer must determine whether a network path exists between two ENIs across complex routing without sending traffic. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
VPC Reachability Analyzer
VPC Flow Logs queries
CloudWatch Synthetics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer analyzes configurations to determine whether a path exists and identifies the blocking component.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Trusted Advisor: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.
• VPC Flow Logs queries: Flow Logs record actual traffic, which requires traffic to flow.
• CloudWatch Synthetics: Synthetics tests endpoints with traffic.

Key takeaway: Analyze network paths without traffic → Reachability Analyzer.

stem: An engineer wants to see whether traffic from a specific IP to an instance is being accepted or rejected. Which source helps?

choices.text: CloudTrail management events for the account
S3 server access logs for the application bucket
AWS Config configuration history for the account
VPC Flow Logs for the instance's network interface

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Flow Logs record accepted and rejected traffic for interfaces, subnets, or VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail management events for the account: CloudTrail records API calls.
• S3 server access logs for the application bucket: S3 access logs cover bucket requests.
• AWS Config configuration history for the account: Config records configuration changes.

Key takeaway: Accepted or rejected traffic → VPC Flow Logs.

stem: Two VPCs are peered, but instances cannot communicate. Security groups allow the traffic. Which TWO items should be checked? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Route tables in both VPCs include routes to the peer CIDR
Both VPCs have an internet gateway attached
CloudFront is configured in front of each VPC
Both VPCs use the same number of subnets
The VPC CIDR blocks do not overlap

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Peering needs routes in both VPCs' route tables and non-overlapping CIDRs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both VPCs have an internet gateway attached: Internet gateways are not needed for peering.
• CloudFront is configured in front of each VPC: CloudFront is unrelated.
• Both VPCs use the same number of subnets: Subnet counts do not matter.

Key takeaway: Peering needs routes on both sides and non-overlapping CIDRs.

stem: A company wants DNS queries for an internal domain to resolve only within its VPCs. Which Route 53 feature fits?

choices.text: A health check attached to each internal record
A public hosted zone with a long record TTL
A private hosted zone associated with the VPCs
A geolocation record for the internal domain

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private hosted zones answer DNS queries only from associated VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A health check attached to each internal record: Health checks monitor endpoints.
• A public hosted zone with a long record TTL: Public zones answer on the internet.
• A geolocation record for the internal domain: Geolocation routes by user location.

Key takeaway: Internal-only DNS → private hosted zones.

stem: Which TWO options connect an on-premises data center to a VPC? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon CloudFront
Amazon Route 53
AWS Site-to-Site VPN
AWS Direct Connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN provides encrypted tunnels over the internet, and Direct Connect provides a dedicated private connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Global Accelerator: Global Accelerator improves global application routing, not on-premises links.
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront is a CDN.
• Amazon Route 53: Route 53 is DNS.

Key takeaway: Hybrid connectivity → Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect.

stem: Users report intermittent 504 errors from an ALB. Targets are healthy but some requests take longer than 60 seconds. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The ALB's security group is missing an outbound rule to the internet
Requests exceed the ALB idle timeout before the target responds
The target group uses HTTP instead of HTTPS for health checks
The Route 53 record for the ALB has a TTL that is too long

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A 504 from an ALB indicates the target did not respond before the timeout; increasing the idle timeout or speeding up the backend helps.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The ALB's security group is missing an…: Outbound internet rules do not cause target timeouts.
• The target group uses HTTP instead of HTTPS…: Health check protocol does not cause timeouts on requests.
• The Route 53 record for the ALB has a TTL…: DNS TTL does not cause 504s.

Key takeaway: ALB 504 = target response exceeded the timeout.

stem: A multiplayer game needs static anycast IP addresses and fast failover between Regions for TCP and UDP traffic. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator
An NLB in one Region
Route 53 simple routing
Amazon CloudFront

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes TCP and UDP traffic over the AWS network to healthy Regional endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An NLB in one Region: One NLB is not multi-Region.
• Route 53 simple routing: Simple routing has no failover and is DNS-based.
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront focuses on HTTP content delivery.

Key takeaway: Static IPs and TCP/UDP multi-Region failover → Global Accelerator.

stem: An application publishes a custom metric that needs one-second granularity for alarms on short spikes. What should the team use?

choices.text: Standard-resolution metrics aggregated every five minutes
High-resolution custom metrics with a 10-second alarm period
VPC Flow Logs aggregated at one-minute intervals
CloudTrail data events on the application's API calls

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High-resolution custom metrics store data at one-second granularity, and alarms on them can evaluate periods as short as 10 seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard-resolution metrics aggregated every…: Five-minute aggregation hides short spikes.
• VPC Flow Logs aggregated at one-minute intervals: Flow Logs capture network traffic, not app metrics.
• CloudTrail data events on the application's…: CloudTrail records API calls, not custom metrics.

Key takeaway: Short spikes need high-resolution metrics.

stem: A team wants to alert when request latency deviates from its usual daily pattern rather than from a fixed threshold. Which CloudWatch feature fits?

choices.text: A dashboard showing the last hour of latency
A metric math expression summing two metrics
Anomaly detection alarms based on a learned band
A static threshold alarm at the average latency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Anomaly detection learns expected patterns and alarms when values leave the expected band.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A dashboard showing the last hour of latency: Dashboards do not alert.
• A metric math expression summing two metrics: Summing metrics does not model patterns.
• A static threshold alarm at the average latency: Static thresholds ignore daily patterns.

Key takeaway: Pattern-aware alerting → anomaly detection alarms.

stem: A team must keep application logs in CloudWatch Logs for 90 days and then delete them automatically. What should they configure?

choices.text: A metric filter that deletes old events
A Lambda function that runs every hour
An S3 lifecycle rule on the log group
A 90-day retention setting on the log group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Log group retention settings automatically expire log events after the chosen period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A metric filter that deletes old events: Metric filters do not delete logs.
• A Lambda function that runs every hour: A custom function is unnecessary.
• An S3 lifecycle rule on the log group: Lifecycle rules apply to S3, not log groups.

Key takeaway: Control log retention on the log group.

stem: A company wants to view metrics and logs from 20 accounts in one monitoring account without copying data. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Separate dashboards in each account
A shared IAM user for all accounts
CloudWatch cross-account observability
Daily exports of all logs to S3

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch cross-account observability links source accounts to a monitoring account to view their telemetry centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate dashboards in each account: Separate dashboards do not centralize.
• A shared IAM user for all accounts: Shared IAM users are insecure.
• Daily exports of all logs to S3: Exports copy data and add delay.

Key takeaway: Centralized multi-account monitoring → cross-account observability.

stem: A team wants to compute an error rate by dividing 5XX errors by total requests and alarm on it. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A log group subscription filter
Metric math in a CloudWatch alarm
A CloudTrail Insights event
A composite alarm on two logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Metric math combines metrics into expressions, such as a ratio, that alarms can evaluate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A log group subscription filter: Subscription filters stream logs.
• A CloudTrail Insights event: CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API activity.
• A composite alarm on two logs: Composite alarms combine alarm states, not metric values.

Key takeaway: Derived metrics such as ratios → metric math.

stem: An EC2 instance's CPU credit balance drops to zero each afternoon and performance falls. The instance is a t3.medium in standard mode. What is a good fix?

choices.text: Switch to unlimited mode or move to a fixed-performance instance type
Increase the size of the instance's root EBS volume by 50 percent
Attach an Elastic IP address to the instance's primary interface
Enable detailed monitoring to publish metrics every minute instead

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Burstable instances throttle when credits run out; unlimited mode or a non-burstable type sustains higher CPU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the size of the instance's root EBS…: Disk size does not affect CPU credits.
• Attach an Elastic IP address to the…: Elastic IPs do not affect performance.
• Enable detailed monitoring to publish…: Monitoring frequency does not add CPU.

Key takeaway: Credit exhaustion on T instances → unlimited mode or a different type.

stem: A company wants to automatically stop development EC2 instances every night at 20:00 to save cost. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A CloudWatch alarm on CPU that terminates any instance below five percent usage
An S3 lifecycle rule attached to the bucket that stores the instances' log files
An IAM policy that denies all EC2 actions after 20:00 for every user in the account
An EventBridge Scheduler schedule that runs an SSM Automation to stop tagged instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A scheduled EventBridge trigger running an Automation runbook can stop instances selected by tags.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A CloudWatch alarm on CPU that terminates…: Termination on low CPU is risky and not time-based.
• An S3 lifecycle rule attached to the bucket…: Lifecycle rules manage S3 objects.
• An IAM policy that denies all EC2 actions…: IAM denies do not stop running instances.

Key takeaway: Scheduled operations → EventBridge Scheduler plus SSM Automation.

stem: A Lambda function that processes S3 uploads intermittently times out. Logs show it runs close to its configured limit. What should be checked first?

choices.text: The CloudFront distribution's cache behavior for uploaded files
The S3 bucket's storage class for older objects in the bucket
The function's timeout and memory settings versus its actual duration
The Route 53 hosted zone used by the function's API endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Timeouts near the limit suggest the timeout is too low or the function needs more memory (which also adds CPU).

Why the other options are wrong:
• The CloudFront distribution's cache behavior…: CloudFront is unrelated to S3-triggered processing.
• The S3 bucket's storage class for older…: Storage class does not cause timeouts.
• The Route 53 hosted zone used by the…: DNS is unrelated here.

Key takeaway: For Lambda timeouts, review timeout and memory settings.

stem: A team wants to trace requests across API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB to find which segment adds latency. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS X-Ray
AWS Batch
AWS Config
Amazon Macie

explanation:
Why this is correct:
X-Ray traces requests across services and shows latency by segment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Batch: Batch runs batch jobs.
• AWS Config: Config records configurations.
• Amazon Macie: Macie finds sensitive data.

Key takeaway: Distributed tracing → AWS X-Ray.

stem: An S3-backed application serves many small requests per second and is throttled with 503 Slow Down errors on one prefix. What helps?

choices.text: Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the whole bucket
Spread objects across more prefixes to parallelize request rates
Disable versioning on the bucket to reduce the number of objects
Change the storage class of all objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 request limits apply per prefix; distributing objects across prefixes increases aggregate throughput.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on…: Object Lock protects objects, not throughput.
• Disable versioning on the bucket to reduce…: Versioning does not affect request limits.
• Change the storage class of all objects to…: Glacier slows access.

Key takeaway: Scale S3 request rates across prefixes.

stem: An RDS for PostgreSQL database hits its connection limit because many Lambda functions open connections. Which service helps?

choices.text: Amazon SQS FIFO
AWS Glue crawlers
Amazon S3 Select
Amazon RDS Proxy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RDS Proxy pools and reuses connections, protecting the database from connection storms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS FIFO: SQS FIFO queues messages.
• AWS Glue crawlers: Glue crawlers catalog data.
• Amazon S3 Select: S3 Select queries objects.

Key takeaway: Connection pooling for bursty clients → RDS Proxy.

stem: A reporting workload slows down an RDS primary database. Which change offloads read queries?

choices.text: Create read replicas and point reporting to them
Enable Multi-AZ and send reports to the standby
Increase the backup retention period to 35 days
Turn on Enhanced Monitoring for the database

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Read replicas serve read traffic, reducing load on the primary.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable Multi-AZ and send reports to the standby: A Multi-AZ instance standby does not serve reads.
• Increase the backup retention period to 35 days: Retention does not affect load.
• Turn on Enhanced Monitoring for the database: Monitoring observes but does not offload.

Key takeaway: Offload reads to read replicas.

stem: An EC2 instance runs a database that needs very high random I/O with sub-millisecond latency, and data can be rebuilt if lost. Which storage fits?

choices.text: Amazon S3 Standard objects
EBS st1 throughput volumes
Instance store NVMe volumes
EBS sc1 cold HDD volumes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instance store provides very low-latency local NVMe storage but is ephemeral, fitting rebuildable data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon S3 Standard objects: S3 is object storage, not block I/O.
• EBS st1 throughput volumes: st1 targets sequential throughput, not random I/O.
• EBS sc1 cold HDD volumes: sc1 is low-cost, low-performance HDD.

Key takeaway: Ephemeral, ultra-low-latency I/O → instance store.

stem: Which TWO actions give visibility into an application's user experience from different geographic locations? (Select TWO)

choices.text: IAM Access Analyzer findings for the application bucket
AWS Config rules on the application's security groups
AWS Backup reports for the application's EBS snapshots
CloudWatch RUM to collect real user performance data
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries run from multiple Regions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Canaries simulate users from chosen locations, and RUM collects performance data from real browsers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM Access Analyzer findings for the…: Access Analyzer checks access.
• AWS Config rules on the application's…: Config rules check configuration.
• AWS Backup reports for the application's EBS…: Backup reports cover backups.

Key takeaway: User experience visibility → Synthetics plus RUM.

stem: A team wants to automatically open an incident and run a response runbook when a critical alarm fires. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector coverage reports
AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection alerts
AWS Trusted Advisor priority checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Incident Manager creates incidents from alarms or events, engages responders, and runs runbooks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Inspector coverage reports: Inspector reports vulnerabilities.
• AWS Cost Anomaly Detection alerts: Cost Anomaly Detection finds unusual spend.
• AWS Trusted Advisor priority checks: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.

Key takeaway: Alarm-driven incident response → Incident Manager.

stem: An EBS-backed database on EC2 shows high I/O wait. CloudWatch shows the volume at its provisioned IOPS limit. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Enable EBS encryption to reduce the number of I/O operations
Increase provisioned IOPS or move to a higher-performance volume type
Detach and reattach the volume to reset the IOPS counter
Snapshot the volume more often to free up I/O capacity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hitting provisioned IOPS means the volume is the bottleneck; raising IOPS or changing volume type relieves it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable EBS encryption to reduce the number…: Encryption does not reduce I/O.
• Detach and reattach the volume to reset the…: Reattaching does not change limits.
• Snapshot the volume more often to free up…: Snapshots add load rather than capacity.

Key takeaway: At the IOPS limit, provision more IOPS or a faster volume type.

stem: An Auto Scaling group keeps terminating and replacing instances right after launch. Instances need three minutes to start the application. What should be adjusted?

choices.text: The maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling group
The instance type used in the launch template
The number of subnets in the Auto Scaling group
The health check grace period for the Auto Scaling group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The grace period delays health checks until instances finish starting, preventing premature replacement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling group: Maximum capacity does not affect health checks.
• The instance type used in the launch template: Instance type does not fix early checks.
• The number of subnets in the Auto Scaling group: Subnet count does not affect health timing.

Key takeaway: Allow startup time with a health check grace period.

stem: Which TWO data sources can CloudWatch Logs subscription filters send log events to in near real time? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AWS Lambda functions
Amazon RDS databases
AWS CloudFormation stacks
Amazon EBS volumes
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Subscription filters can deliver logs to Kinesis Data Streams, Data Firehose, Lambda, or OpenSearch Service.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon RDS databases: RDS is not a subscription destination.
• AWS CloudFormation stacks: CloudFormation is not a destination.
• Amazon EBS volumes: EBS is block storage, not a destination.

Key takeaway: Stream logs with subscription filters to Kinesis, Firehose, Lambda, or OpenSearch.

stem: A company runs a steady-state fleet of EC2 instances 24/7 for three years and wants to cut compute cost without changing instances often. Which option fits?

choices.text: On-Demand Instances only, since commitments never reduce long-term cost
Spot Instances for all production instances without interruption handling
Compute Savings Plans or Reserved Instances for the steady usage
Dedicated Hosts for every instance to share costs across other accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Commitments such as Savings Plans or Reserved Instances significantly reduce cost for steady, predictable usage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-Demand Instances only, since commitments…: Commitments do reduce steady-state cost.
• Spot Instances for all production instances…: Spot can be interrupted and needs handling.
• Dedicated Hosts for every instance to share…: Dedicated Hosts are for licensing or isolation, not cost sharing.

Key takeaway: Steady usage → Savings Plans or Reserved Instances.

stem: A team wants to understand unexpected cost increases in their account by service and date. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Config history
VPC Reachability Analyzer
CloudWatch Logs Insights

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cost Explorer visualizes and filters costs by service, time, and tags to find drivers of increases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config history: Config history tracks configuration changes.
• VPC Reachability Analyzer: Reachability Analyzer checks network paths.
• CloudWatch Logs Insights: Logs Insights queries logs.

Key takeaway: Analyze spending with Cost Explorer.

stem: A company wants to be alerted when monthly spending is forecast to exceed its budget. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config compliance timeline
AWS Artifact report downloads
AWS Budgets with a forecast alert
Amazon Inspector coverage alerts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Budgets can alert on actual or forecasted spend exceeding thresholds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config compliance timeline: Config tracks compliance, not spend.
• AWS Artifact report downloads: Artifact provides compliance reports.
• Amazon Inspector coverage alerts: Inspector reports vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: Spend alerts → AWS Budgets.

stem: A queue-based worker fleet on EC2 should grow when messages pile up. Which metric is the best basis for scaling?

choices.text: Average disk space used by each worker
Backlog per instance derived from queue depth
Number of CloudTrail events per minute
Total number of instances in the account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scaling on backlog per instance (queue depth divided by instance count) matches capacity to pending work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Average disk space used by each worker: Disk usage is unrelated to queue load.
• Number of CloudTrail events per minute: CloudTrail events do not reflect workload.
• Total number of instances in the account: Instance count is not a demand signal.

Key takeaway: Scale queue workers on backlog per instance.

stem: A company wants EC2 capacity at the lowest cost for a fault-tolerant batch workload that can handle interruptions. Which option fits?

choices.text: Reserved Instances for a single instance size
On-Demand Instances in a single instance type
Dedicated Instances in one Availability Zone
Spot Instances with diversified instance types

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spot offers large discounts; diversifying types and pools reduces interruption impact for tolerant workloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reserved Instances for a single instance size: Reservations suit steady usage, not flexible batch.
• On-Demand Instances in a single instance type: On-Demand costs more.
• Dedicated Instances in one Availability Zone: Dedicated Instances cost more and do not reduce interruptions.

Key takeaway: Interruption-tolerant work → diversified Spot.

stem: An Aurora cluster's read traffic varies a lot throughout the day. The team wants reader count to follow demand. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Aurora Global Database secondary Regions
Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas
Aurora Backtrack on the writer instance
Aurora cloning of the production cluster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes replicas based on metrics such as CPU or connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Aurora Global Database secondary Regions: Global Database is for cross-Region DR and reads.
• Aurora Backtrack on the writer instance: Backtrack rewinds data.
• Aurora cloning of the production cluster: Cloning creates copies for testing.

Key takeaway: Scale Aurora readers automatically with Aurora Auto Scaling.

stem: An application needs a relational database that survives an AZ failure with minimal data loss and faster failover than a single standby instance. Which option fits?

choices.text: DynamoDB with a single-partition table design
A self-managed database on one EC2 instance
Aurora with replicas in multiple Availability Zones
RDS single-AZ instance with daily snapshots

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora stores data across three AZs and can fail over to an Aurora Replica quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamoDB with a single-partition table design: DynamoDB is not relational.
• A self-managed database on one EC2 instance: A single instance is a single point of failure.
• RDS single-AZ instance with daily snapshots: Single-AZ lacks automatic failover.

Key takeaway: Fast relational failover across AZs → Aurora with replicas.

stem: A company's critical application must survive a full Region outage with minimal downtime for its DynamoDB data. Which feature fits?

choices.text: DynamoDB global tables across two Regions
DynamoDB TTL for automatic item expiry
DynamoDB on-demand backups in one Region
DynamoDB Accelerator in the primary Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global tables replicate data across Regions and allow reads and writes in each, supporting Regional failover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamoDB TTL for automatic item expiry: TTL deletes items.
• DynamoDB on-demand backups in one Region: Same-Region backups do not survive Region loss quickly.
• DynamoDB Accelerator in the primary Region: DAX caches within one Region.

Key takeaway: Multi-Region DynamoDB resilience → global tables.

stem: An NLB-fronted service in two AZs should keep serving if one AZ loses all targets. Which setting helps distribute traffic across the remaining healthy targets?

choices.text: TLS termination on the listener
Sticky sessions on the target group
A longer deregistration delay
Cross-zone load balancing enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-zone load balancing lets each load balancer node route to healthy targets in all enabled AZs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TLS termination on the listener: TLS termination does not affect distribution.
• Sticky sessions on the target group: Stickiness pins clients but does not fix AZ imbalance.
• A longer deregistration delay: Deregistration delay affects draining.

Key takeaway: Spread traffic across AZs with cross-zone load balancing.

stem: A stateful web app loses user sessions when instances are replaced. Which change improves resilience?

choices.text: Increase the minimum size of the Auto Scaling group
Store session state externally in ElastiCache or DynamoDB
Enable sticky sessions permanently with no expiration
Use larger instances so that fewer are ever replaced

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Externalizing sessions lets any instance serve any user, so replacement does not lose state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the minimum size of the Auto…: More instances do not preserve state on replacement.
• Enable sticky sessions permanently with no…: Stickiness still loses sessions on replacement.
• Use larger instances so that fewer are ever…: Fewer replacements do not eliminate the problem.

Key takeaway: Make instances stateless by externalizing sessions.

stem: A company needs EBS snapshots of tagged volumes every six hours, kept for 14 days, with minimal management. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy
S3 Lifecycle rules on the snapshots
CloudTrail Lake queries on volumes
A manual snapshot runbook each shift

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data Lifecycle Manager automates EBS snapshot creation and retention by tags and schedules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Lifecycle rules on the snapshots: Snapshots are not managed by S3 Lifecycle rules.
• CloudTrail Lake queries on volumes: Queries do not create snapshots.
• A manual snapshot runbook each shift: Manual runbooks are error-prone.

Key takeaway: Automate EBS snapshots with Data Lifecycle Manager.

stem: A company must be able to restore EC2 backups in a second Region if the primary Region fails. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: EBS snapshots shared with another account in the Region
AMIs kept only in the primary Region's default account
An AWS Backup plan with a cross-Region copy rule
A backup plan that keeps copies in the same Region only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-Region copy rules place recovery points in another Region for disaster recovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS snapshots shared with another account in…: Same-Region sharing does not help Region loss.
• AMIs kept only in the primary Region's…: AMIs in one Region are not available elsewhere.
• A backup plan that keeps copies in the same…: Same-Region copies do not survive a Regional outage.

Key takeaway: Regional DR for backups → cross-Region copies.

stem: A team must regularly verify that backups can actually be restored. Which AWS Backup feature helps?

choices.text: Vault access policies
Legal hold settings
Backup audit logs only
Restore testing plans

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Backup restore testing periodically restores recovery points to validate recoverability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Vault access policies: Access policies control vault access.
• Legal hold settings: Legal holds prevent deletion.
• Backup audit logs only: Logs show activity but do not test restores.

Key takeaway: Prove backups work with restore testing.

stem: A company compares DR strategies. It needs recovery within hours and wants low cost. Which strategy fits?

choices.text: Backup and restore or pilot light
Multi-site active-active in two Regions
No DR plan, relying on AWS availability
Warm standby at full production size

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Backup and restore or pilot light keep costs low while meeting recovery objectives of hours.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-site active-active in two Regions: Active-active is the most expensive and exceeds the need.
• No DR plan, relying on AWS availability: No plan risks long outages.
• Warm standby at full production size: Full-size warm standby costs more than needed.

Key takeaway: Match DR strategy to RTO/RPO and budget.

stem: An S3 bucket's critical data must also exist in another Region for disaster recovery. Which feature fits?

choices.text: S3 Storage Lens metrics
S3 Same-Region Replication
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Cross-Region Replication

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-Region Replication copies new objects to a bucket in another Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Storage Lens metrics: Storage Lens reports usage.
• S3 Same-Region Replication: Same-Region Replication stays in one Region.
• S3 Transfer Acceleration: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads.

Key takeaway: Regional DR copies of S3 data → CRR.

stem: Which TWO practices help an Auto Scaling group recover quickly from instance failures? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Set the desired capacity to zero during business hours
Spread instances across multiple Availability Zones
Hard-code instance IP addresses in the application
Disable all health checks to avoid replacements
Use a launch template with a working, current AMI

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A valid launch template enables fast replacements, and multi-AZ spreading limits the impact of AZ issues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Set the desired capacity to zero during…: Zero capacity removes the application.
• Hard-code instance IP addresses in the…: Hard-coded IPs break when instances are replaced.
• Disable all health checks to avoid replacements: Without health checks, failures are not replaced.

Key takeaway: Reliable replacements need good templates and multi-AZ placement.

stem: Which TWO measures reduce single points of failure in a web architecture? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A single on-premises DNS server for resolution
A single NAT instance for all private subnets
A Multi-AZ database deployment
One EC2 instance hosting the entire application
An Application Load Balancer across multiple AZs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A multi-AZ load balancer and a Multi-AZ database remove single points of failure in the web and data tiers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A single on-premises DNS server for resolution: A single DNS server is a single point of failure.
• A single NAT instance for all private subnets: A single NAT instance is a single point of failure.
• One EC2 instance hosting the entire application: One instance is a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: Remove single points of failure in every tier.

stem: Private subnets in three AZs route to a single NAT gateway in one AZ. What is the reliability concern?

choices.text: NAT gateways cannot be used from more than one subnet at a time
Private subnets cannot route to NAT gateways in other AZs at all
If that AZ fails, the other AZs lose outbound internet access
NAT gateways must be recreated every day to keep them working

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway is zonal; for resilience, deploy one per AZ with each AZ's subnets routing to its local gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT gateways cannot be used from more than…: Multiple subnets can use one NAT gateway.
• Private subnets cannot route to NAT gateways…: Cross-AZ routing works but creates the dependency.
• NAT gateways must be recreated every day to…: No daily recreation is needed.

Key takeaway: Deploy a NAT gateway per AZ for resilience.

stem: A company defines the maximum acceptable data loss after an outage as 15 minutes. Which objective is this?

choices.text: Mean time between failures
Recovery point objective
Service level indicator
Recovery time objective

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Mean time between failures: MTBF measures reliability between failures.
• Service level indicator: An SLI is a measured service metric.
• Recovery time objective: RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime.

Key takeaway: RPO = data loss tolerance; RTO = downtime tolerance.

stem: An application's load is predictable each week, and the team wants Auto Scaling to learn this pattern and provision ahead of time. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Predictive scaling
Manual scaling
Lifecycle hooks
Step scaling

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Predictive scaling forecasts load from historical patterns and schedules capacity ahead of demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual scaling: Manual scaling is not automatic.
• Lifecycle hooks: Lifecycle hooks run actions at launch or termination.
• Step scaling: Step scaling reacts to alarms.

Key takeaway: Learned recurring patterns → predictive scaling.

stem: Before an instance is terminated during scale-in, it must upload logs to S3. Which feature allows this?

choices.text: A scheduled action that runs every five minutes
Termination protection enabled for the instance
A longer cooldown period on the scale-in policy
An Auto Scaling lifecycle hook on termination

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lifecycle hooks pause instances in a wait state so custom actions can complete before termination.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A scheduled action that runs every five minutes: Schedules are not tied to termination events.
• Termination protection enabled for the instance: Termination protection blocks scale-in termination entirely.
• A longer cooldown period on the scale-in policy: Cooldowns delay scaling but do not run actions.

Key takeaway: Run actions before termination with lifecycle hooks.

stem: A company must restore an Aurora MySQL database to its state 20 minutes ago after a bad update, quickly and in place. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A manual snapshot from last week
Aurora cloning
A cross-Region read replica
Aurora Backtrack

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Backtrack rewinds an Aurora MySQL cluster to a prior point in time without restoring from a backup.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A manual snapshot from last week: A week-old snapshot loses newer data.
• Aurora cloning: Cloning creates a copy, not a rewind.
• A cross-Region read replica: Replicas replicate the bad update.

Key takeaway: Rewind Aurora MySQL in place with Backtrack.

stem: A company's static website must stay available even if a single S3 Region has issues. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Enable S3 versioning in the single Region's bucket only
Use S3 One Zone-IA storage class for the website files
Replicate to a second Region and use CloudFront origin failover
Serve the website from a single EC2 instance instead

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A replicated bucket in another Region plus CloudFront origin failover keeps the site available if the primary origin fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable S3 versioning in the single Region's…: Versioning does not add Regional redundancy.
• Use S3 One Zone-IA storage class for the…: One Zone-IA reduces availability.
• Serve the website from a single EC2 instance…: One instance is a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: Regional resilience for static sites → CRR plus origin failover.

stem: Which TWO items should a disaster recovery runbook include? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Step-by-step recovery procedures with owners
Marketing copy for the company's public website
A list of all employees' favorite programming languages
The office seating chart for the operations team
Regular tests that validate RTO and RPO

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clear procedures with owners and regular testing ensure recovery works within objectives.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Marketing copy for the company's public website: Marketing copy is irrelevant.
• A list of all employees' favorite…: Language preferences are irrelevant.
• The office seating chart for the operations team: Seating charts are irrelevant.

Key takeaway: DR runbooks need owned procedures and regular tests.

stem: A Lambda function occasionally throttles during bursts and must always have capacity reserved for it. Which setting fits?

choices.text: A longer function timeout setting
Reserved concurrency for the function
A larger memory size for the function
A dead-letter queue for failed events

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reserved concurrency guarantees a portion of account concurrency for the function.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A longer function timeout setting: Timeout does not reserve capacity.
• A larger memory size for the function: Memory affects performance, not concurrency guarantees.
• A dead-letter queue for failed events: A DLQ captures failures but does not prevent throttling.

Key takeaway: Guarantee Lambda capacity with reserved concurrency.

stem: A team wants new EC2 instances to install packages and start an application automatically at first boot. Which mechanism fits?

choices.text: User data scripts or cloud-init in the launch template
An IAM role attached to the Auto Scaling group itself
A Route 53 health check pointed at the instance's IP
A CloudWatch alarm on the instance's CPU utilization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
User data runs scripts at launch to configure instances automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An IAM role attached to the Auto Scaling…: IAM roles grant permissions, not configuration.
• A Route 53 health check pointed at the…: Health checks test endpoints.
• A CloudWatch alarm on the instance's CPU…: Alarms monitor metrics.

Key takeaway: Bootstrap instances with user data.

stem: A CloudFormation template needs the latest Amazon Linux AMI ID in each Region without hard-coding IDs. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A mapping table updated manually each month with AMI IDs
A hard-coded AMI ID copied from the console in one Region and reused in all Regions
A parameter of type SSM parameter pointing to the public AMI alias
A Lambda function that guesses the newest AMI by its name

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation can resolve public Systems Manager parameters for the latest AMI IDs in each Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A mapping table updated manually each month…: Manual mappings go stale.
• A hard-coded AMI ID copied from the console…: Hard-coded IDs are Region-specific and stale.
• A Lambda function that guesses the newest…: Guessing is unreliable.

Key takeaway: Resolve current AMI IDs via SSM public parameters.

stem: A CloudFormation stack must keep its RDS database when the stack is deleted. Which attribute fits?

choices.text: A stack output with the endpoint
DeletionPolicy set to Retain or Snapshot
A condition that is always false
UpdateReplacePolicy set to Delete on the database

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DeletionPolicy controls what happens to a resource when the stack is deleted; Retain keeps it and Snapshot saves a final snapshot.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A stack output with the endpoint: Outputs do not protect resources.
• A condition that is always false: A false condition would prevent creation.
• UpdateReplacePolicy set to Delete on the…: UpdateReplacePolicy governs replacement during updates, and Delete removes it.

Key takeaway: Protect data on stack deletion with DeletionPolicy.

stem: A CloudFormation stack creation hangs waiting for an EC2 instance, then fails after an hour. The template uses a CreationPolicy. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The instance type is unavailable in every Availability Zone
The stack policy denied creation of the EC2 instance resource
The template's outputs section references a missing export
The instance never sent the success signal with cfn-signal

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CreationPolicy waits for a success signal; if cfn-signal is not sent, the stack times out and fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The instance type is unavailable in every…: Unavailable types fail immediately.
• The stack policy denied creation of the EC2…: Stack policies apply to updates, not creation.
• The template's outputs section references a…: Missing exports fail differently and quickly.

Key takeaway: CreationPolicy needs cfn-signal to report success.

stem: A team wants to share VPC ID and subnet IDs from one stack for use in other stacks. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Tags applied at the stack level only
Change sets reviewed before execution
Stack policies with an Allow statement for all resources
Stack outputs with Export and Fn::ImportValue

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exported outputs can be imported by other stacks in the same Region with Fn::ImportValue.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tags applied at the stack level only: Tags label resources.
• Change sets reviewed before execution: Change sets preview updates.
• Stack policies with an Allow statement for…: Stack policies protect resources.

Key takeaway: Share values across stacks with exports and ImportValue.

stem: A company wants developers to launch only approved, preconfigured products, such as a standard EC2 web stack, without broad permissions. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Service Catalog
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS License Manager
AWS Resource Groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service Catalog offers approved CloudFormation-based products that users can launch with constrained permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Trusted Advisor: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.
• AWS License Manager: License Manager tracks licenses.
• AWS Resource Groups: Resource Groups organize resources.

Key takeaway: Self-service approved products → Service Catalog.

stem: A team deploys a web application and wants AWS to handle capacity provisioning, load balancing, and health monitoring with minimal configuration. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Storage Gateway
Amazon Route 53 Resolver
AWS Elastic Beanstalk
AWS Direct Connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Beanstalk deploys and manages web applications, handling provisioning, load balancing, and scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Storage Gateway: Storage Gateway connects on-premises storage.
• Amazon Route 53 Resolver: Resolver handles DNS resolution.
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect provides network links.

Key takeaway: Managed app deployment with minimal setup → Elastic Beanstalk.

stem: An Elastic Beanstalk update must not reduce capacity and should roll back quickly if new instances fail. Which deployment policy fits?

choices.text: In-place single batch
Immutable deployment
Rolling without batches
All at once deployment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable deployments launch new instances in a temporary group, keeping full capacity and allowing quick rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In-place single batch: In-place updates reduce capacity and are harder to roll back.
• Rolling without batches: Rolling reduces capacity during updates.
• All at once deployment: All at once causes downtime.

Key takeaway: Full capacity and easy rollback → immutable deployments.

stem: A team wants to trigger an automated fix whenever an EBS volume is created without encryption. Which combination fits?

choices.text: An EventBridge rule or Config rule that invokes an SSM Automation runbook
A monthly CSV export of volumes reviewed by the security team
A Route 53 health check on the EC2 instance using the volume
A CloudFront distribution that caches the current volume list for the operations users

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Event- or Config-based detection that triggers Automation runbooks enables automated remediation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A monthly CSV export of volumes reviewed by…: Monthly reviews are slow and manual.
• A Route 53 health check on the EC2 instance…: Health checks do not inspect volumes.
• A CloudFront distribution that caches the…: CloudFront is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Detect and remediate with events and Automation runbooks.

stem: A company wants to run scheduled maintenance tasks, such as Run Command documents, on groups of instances only during approved hours. Which feature fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs retention settings
AWS Config aggregator schedules
EC2 Instance Scheduler on Lambda only
Systems Manager Maintenance Windows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Maintenance Windows define schedules and targets for running tasks such as Run Command and Automation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch Logs retention settings: Retention settings manage logs.
• AWS Config aggregator schedules: Aggregators collect Config data.
• EC2 Instance Scheduler on Lambda only: Instance scheduling starts and stops instances but is not a task window.

Key takeaway: Schedule operational tasks with Maintenance Windows.

stem: EC2 instances are not appearing as managed instances in Systems Manager. Which TWO items should be checked? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The instances have Elastic IP addresses associated
The instance profile includes the required SSM permissions
The instances have termination protection enabled
The instances use the largest available instance type
The SSM Agent is installed and running on the instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed instances need a running SSM Agent, permissions (such as AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore), and network access to SSM endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The instances have Elastic IP addresses…: Elastic IPs are not required.
• The instances have termination protection…: Termination protection is irrelevant.
• The instances use the largest available…: Instance size is irrelevant.

Key takeaway: SSM management needs the agent, permissions, and connectivity.

stem: A private subnet with no internet access hosts instances that must be managed by Systems Manager. What is required?

choices.text: An internet gateway attached to the private subnet's route table
A public IP address assigned to each instance at launch
Interface VPC endpoints for SSM, SSM messages, and EC2 messages
A VPC peering connection to a public subnet in another VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Without internet access, instances reach Systems Manager through interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An internet gateway attached to the private…: That would make the subnet public.
• A public IP address assigned to each…: Public IPs require internet routing.
• A VPC peering connection to a public subnet…: Peering does not provide access to AWS service endpoints.

Key takeaway: Private SSM access → interface endpoints.

stem: A team wants to update the AMI used by an Auto Scaling group and gradually replace running instances. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Termination protection on every existing instance
Instance refresh with the updated launch template
Detaching all instances and launching them manually
A scheduled scaling action to zero at midnight

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instance refresh replaces instances in batches according to minimum healthy percentage, using the new launch template.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Termination protection on every existing…: Termination protection blocks replacement.
• Detaching all instances and launching them…: Manual replacement is error-prone.
• A scheduled scaling action to zero at midnight: Scaling to zero causes an outage.

Key takeaway: Roll out new AMIs with instance refresh.

stem: A team must create identical test environments frequently and tear them down after use. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Define the environment in CloudFormation and create or delete stacks
Keep one permanent test environment that everyone shares forever
Copy production data and servers manually for each test cycle
Build each environment manually in the console and delete by hand

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Infrastructure as code creates repeatable environments and deletes all resources together.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep one permanent test environment that…: A shared permanent environment causes conflicts.
• Copy production data and servers manually…: Manual copying is error-prone.
• Build each environment manually in the…: Manual builds are slow and inconsistent.

Key takeaway: Repeatable environments come from IaC.
