stem: A company needs to share an AMI with another AWS account securely. The AMI uses encrypted EBS snapshots. What must also be shared?

choices.text: The root user password of the source account that owns the AMI
The CloudTrail trail of the source account
Access to the KMS key used to encrypt the snapshots
The VPC and subnets where the AMI was built

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Encrypted AMIs require the target account to have permission to use the KMS key (a customer managed key).

Why the other options are wrong:
• The root user password of the source account…: Root passwords must never be shared.
• The CloudTrail trail of the source account: CloudTrail is unrelated.
• The VPC and subnets where the AMI was built: Networks are not needed to share AMIs.

Key takeaway: Sharing encrypted AMIs requires KMS key access.

stem: A company deploys containers and wants AWS to manage the servers entirely while it defines only tasks and services. Which option fits?

choices.text: Amazon ECS on self-managed EC2
Kubernetes on on-premises VMs
Docker on a single EC2 host
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fargate runs containers without managing servers or clusters of instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon ECS on self-managed EC2: EC2 launch type requires managing instances.
• Kubernetes on on-premises VMs: On-premises VMs require full management.
• Docker on a single EC2 host: A single host must be managed and is a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: Serverless containers → Fargate.

stem: A team wants every S3 bucket created in the account to have default encryption and tags, enforced automatically. Which TWO mechanisms help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: CloudFormation templates or Service Catalog products used for bucket creation
Disabling CloudTrail so creations are not logged
A dashboard listing bucket names by creation date
A weekly email reminding engineers to add tags
AWS Config rules with automatic remediation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standardized templates build compliant buckets, and Config rules catch and fix buckets created outside them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling CloudTrail so creations are not logged: Disabling logs removes auditing.
• A dashboard listing bucket names by creation…: Dashboards do not enforce settings.
• A weekly email reminding engineers to add tags: Reminders are not enforcement.

Key takeaway: Enforce standards with templates plus detective remediation.

stem: A CloudFormation stack deletion fails because an S3 bucket in the stack still contains objects. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Add a new tag to the bucket and try the deletion one more time
Delete the AWS account that owns the stack and the bucket
Change the bucket's storage class to S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Empty the bucket, or retain it, and then retry the deletion

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation cannot delete non-empty buckets; emptying them (or retaining them) allows deletion to proceed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Add a new tag to the bucket and try the…: Tags do not remove objects.
• Delete the AWS account that owns the stack…: Deleting the account is drastic.
• Change the bucket's storage class to S3…: Storage class does not affect deletion.

Key takeaway: Empty or retain S3 buckets before deleting stacks.

stem: A company wants configuration changes to Lambda-based operational scripts to go through code review and automatic deployment. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Email code changes to an administrator who pastes them into Lambda
Store the code in a repository with a CodePipeline that deploys on merge
Keep scripts only on one engineer's laptop and upload them manually
Edit functions directly in the console during production incidents

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A version-controlled repository with an automated pipeline provides review, traceability, and consistent deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Email code changes to an administrator who…: Emailing code is error-prone.
• Keep scripts only on one engineer's laptop…: Laptop-only scripts are fragile and unreviewed.
• Edit functions directly in the console…: Console edits bypass review.

Key takeaway: Manage operational code through version control and pipelines.

stem: A team needs to provision the same resources in multiple Regions from one CloudFormation template, with Region-specific values such as instance types. Which template feature fits?

choices.text: Stack policies that deny all updates to resources
DependsOn attributes between all resources
Mappings keyed by Region with Fn::FindInMap
Outputs exported under the same name everywhere

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mappings provide lookup tables, such as Region-specific values, retrieved with Fn::FindInMap.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stack policies that deny all updates to…: Stack policies protect resources.
• DependsOn attributes between all resources: DependsOn controls order.
• Outputs exported under the same name everywhere: Outputs expose values; export names must be unique per Region.

Key takeaway: Region-specific values → Mappings and FindInMap.

stem: A company wants to patch only instances tagged Environment=Dev first, then Prod a week later. Which Patch Manager approach fits?

choices.text: Disabling patching for Prod entirely to avoid any application risk
One maintenance window that patches every instance in all accounts and environments at once
Manual patching of each instance by logging in over SSH each week
Separate patch groups or targets by tag with different maintenance windows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Targeting by tags with separate windows lets teams stage patching from Dev to Prod.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling patching for Prod entirely to…: Skipping Prod patches leaves vulnerabilities.
• One maintenance window that patches every…: Patching everything at once removes staging.
• Manual patching of each instance by logging…: Manual patching does not scale.

Key takeaway: Stage patching with tag-based targets and windows.

stem: A company wants to test how its application behaves when an Availability Zone becomes unavailable, in a controlled way. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Fault Injection Service
AWS Trusted Advisor checks
AWS Compute Optimizer
Amazon Inspector

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fault Injection Service runs controlled experiments, such as AZ disruptions, to test resilience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Trusted Advisor checks: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.
• AWS Compute Optimizer: Compute Optimizer recommends sizes.
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector finds vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: Test resilience with Fault Injection Service.

stem: A company wants a single sign-on experience for employees accessing multiple AWS accounts with centrally managed permissions. Which service fits?

choices.text: IAM users in every account
Amazon Cognito user pools
AWS IAM Identity Center
AWS Directory Service only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center provides SSO across accounts with permission sets assigned centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM users in every account: Per-account IAM users do not provide SSO and are hard to manage.
• Amazon Cognito user pools: Cognito targets customer-facing application users.
• AWS Directory Service only: Directory Service alone does not assign AWS account permissions.

Key takeaway: Workforce SSO across accounts → IAM Identity Center.

stem: An application on EC2 needs to read from a DynamoDB table. What is the most secure way to give it credentials?

choices.text: Access keys stored in the application's config file
An IAM role attached through an instance profile
The root user's access keys set as environment variables
A shared IAM user's password hard-coded into the code

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instance profiles deliver temporary, automatically rotated credentials from an IAM role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access keys stored in the application's…: Stored long-term keys can leak.
• The root user's access keys set as…: Root keys must never be used this way.
• A shared IAM user's password hard-coded into…: Hard-coded passwords are insecure.

Key takeaway: Give EC2 access through IAM roles, not stored keys.

stem: A security team wants all API activity from every account in the organization recorded to one central bucket. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: A separate trail in only the management account
An organization trail in AWS CloudTrail
VPC Flow Logs for every VPC in the organization
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries in each account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An organization trail logs events for all member accounts to a central location.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A separate trail in only the management account: A management-account trail alone does not cover members unless it is an organization trail.
• VPC Flow Logs for every VPC in the organization: Flow Logs capture network traffic, not API calls.
• CloudWatch Logs Insights queries in each account: Queries do not record events.

Key takeaway: Organization-wide API logging → organization trail.

stem: Security must detect and alert whenever the root user signs in to any account. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A CloudWatch dashboard showing the number of IAM users per account
A monthly review of IAM credential reports by the security team
An EventBridge rule on root sign-in events from CloudTrail with an SNS target
An AWS Config rule that checks S3 bucket encryption settings daily

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records console sign-in events; an EventBridge rule can match root sign-ins and notify through SNS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A CloudWatch dashboard showing the number of…: User counts do not detect sign-ins.
• A monthly review of IAM credential reports…: Monthly reviews are too slow.
• An AWS Config rule that checks S3 bucket…: Encryption checks are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Alert on root sign-ins with CloudTrail events and EventBridge.

stem: A company must encrypt data in an S3 bucket with keys it controls and audit every key use. Which option fits?

choices.text: No encryption with bucket versioning
SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys
Client-side encryption with no key logs
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key gives control over key policies and logs key usage in CloudTrail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No encryption with bucket versioning: Versioning is not encryption.
• SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3 without customer control.
• Client-side encryption with no key logs: No logging fails the audit requirement.

Key takeaway: Controlled, auditable S3 encryption → SSE-KMS with a CMK.

stem: A company wants to protect its public web application from large DDoS attacks, with access to the AWS response team and cost protection. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Shield Advanced
AWS Shield Standard
Network ACLs only
Security groups only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS protection, access to the Shield Response Team, and cost protection for scaling during attacks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Shield Standard: Shield Standard provides baseline protection without those features.
• Network ACLs only: NACLs cannot absorb large DDoS attacks.
• Security groups only: Security groups do not stop DDoS attacks.

Key takeaway: Enhanced DDoS protection and support → Shield Advanced.

stem: A company needs TLS certificates for its ALBs that renew automatically. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Secrets Manager rotating certificate text
AWS Certificate Manager public certificates
Certificates stored in an S3 bucket manually
Self-signed certificates on each EC2 instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM issues and automatically renews public certificates for integrated services such as ALB.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Secrets Manager rotating certificate text: Secrets Manager stores secrets but does not issue public certificates.
• Certificates stored in an S3 bucket manually: Manual storage lacks renewal.
• Self-signed certificates on each EC2 instance: Self-signed certificates are not trusted by browsers.

Key takeaway: Auto-renewing certificates for ALBs → ACM.

stem: Which TWO controls help protect EC2 instances in a web tier? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Public IPs and open SSH from anywhere on every instance
Disabling OS patching to avoid application changes
Security groups allowing only required ports from the ALB
Shared access keys stored on each instance's disk
Private subnets for instances behind the load balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Least-privilege security groups and private placement behind the ALB reduce the attack surface.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IPs and open SSH from anywhere on…: Open SSH exposes instances.
• Disabling OS patching to avoid application…: Unpatched systems are vulnerable.
• Shared access keys stored on each instance's…: Stored shared keys can leak.

Key takeaway: Limit exposure with tight security groups and private subnets.

stem: A company must keep AWS Config recording enabled in every account and Region of its organization. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Deploy Config with StackSets and deny StopConfigurationRecorder with an SCP
Ask each account owner to check Config settings once per year
Enable Config only in the management account's home Region
Store Config data in a public S3 bucket for easy access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
StackSets deploy Config everywhere, and an SCP prevents member accounts from stopping the recorder.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ask each account owner to check Config…: Annual checks are not enforcement.
• Enable Config only in the management…: One account and Region is insufficient.
• Store Config data in a public S3 bucket for…: Public buckets expose data.

Key takeaway: Deploy widely with StackSets and lock with SCPs.

stem: An auditor needs evidence that KMS keys used for production data are rotated. What should the operations team enable?

choices.text: Manual key deletion every 30 days for all keys
Disabling CloudTrail logging for KMS API calls
Key sharing with all accounts in the organization
Automatic key rotation for the customer managed keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automatic rotation for customer managed keys generates new key material on a schedule, and rotation status can be shown to auditors.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual key deletion every 30 days for all keys: Deleting keys makes encrypted data unreadable.
• Disabling CloudTrail logging for KMS API calls: Disabling logs removes evidence.
• Key sharing with all accounts in the…: Sharing keys widely increases risk.

Key takeaway: Enable automatic rotation for customer managed KMS keys.

stem: A team wants to investigate the root cause of a GuardDuty finding by analyzing related activity over time. Which service helps?

choices.text: Amazon Detective
AWS DataSync
Amazon Polly
Amazon Lightsail

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detective organizes log data into graphs that help investigate security findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS DataSync: DataSync transfers data.
• Amazon Polly: Polly synthesizes speech.
• Amazon Lightsail: Lightsail hosts simple applications.

Key takeaway: Investigate findings with Amazon Detective.

stem: A company wants to manage WAF rules and Shield protections consistently across all accounts in its organization. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Resource Groups
AWS Firewall Manager
AWS Cloud Map
AWS Health Dashboard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firewall Manager centrally configures WAF, Shield Advanced, security groups, and Network Firewall across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Resource Groups: Resource Groups organize resources.
• AWS Cloud Map: Cloud Map handles service discovery.
• AWS Health Dashboard: The Health Dashboard shows service events.

Key takeaway: Central firewall policy across accounts → Firewall Manager.

stem: Which TWO practices strengthen IAM security for human users? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Keep unused access keys active forever
Share one admin user among the team
Require MFA for console sign-in
Grant AdministratorAccess to every user
Use temporary credentials through roles

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MFA protects sign-ins, and temporary credentials via roles avoid long-lived keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep unused access keys active forever: Unused keys increase risk.
• Share one admin user among the team: Shared users remove accountability.
• Grant AdministratorAccess to every user: Broad permissions violate least privilege.

Key takeaway: Use MFA and temporary credentials.

stem: A company needs a dedicated, consistent-bandwidth private connection from its data center to AWS. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront
AWS Client VPN
AWS Site-to-Site VPN
AWS Direct Connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity with consistent performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront is a CDN.
• AWS Client VPN: Client VPN connects individual users.
• AWS Site-to-Site VPN: VPN runs over the internet with variable performance.

Key takeaway: Dedicated, consistent private link → Direct Connect.

stem: A Direct Connect link must have a backup path if it fails, at low cost. Which option fits?

choices.text: A CloudFront distribution in front of the VPC
A second VPC with no hybrid connectivity
An internet gateway on the on-premises side
A Site-to-Site VPN as a backup connection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A VPN over the internet is a common low-cost backup for Direct Connect.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A CloudFront distribution in front of the VPC: CloudFront does not provide hybrid connectivity.
• A second VPC with no hybrid connectivity: Another VPC does not connect on-premises.
• An internet gateway on the on-premises side: Internet gateways are AWS VPC components.

Key takeaway: Back up Direct Connect with a Site-to-Site VPN.

stem: Remote employees need secure access to resources in a VPC from their laptops. Which service fits?

choices.text: VPC peering links
AWS Direct Connect
AWS Client VPN
NAT gateways only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Client VPN provides managed remote-access VPN for users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering links: Peering connects VPCs.
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect links data centers, not individual laptops.
• NAT gateways only: NAT gateways provide outbound internet access.

Key takeaway: Remote user access to VPCs → Client VPN.

stem: A company wants to split traffic 90/10 between the current and new versions of its application using DNS. Which Route 53 policy fits?

choices.text: Weighted routing
Failover routing
Geolocation routing
Latency routing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing distributes traffic by assigned weights.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Failover routing: Failover routes by health.
• Geolocation routing: Geolocation routes by location.
• Latency routing: Latency routing uses network latency.

Key takeaway: Percentage-based DNS traffic split → weighted routing.

stem: A CloudFront distribution must serve personalized API responses and cached static assets from the same domain. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: One cache behavior with a 24-hour TTL for every request
Separate cache behaviors by path with different caching settings
Disable caching for the entire distribution's traffic
Use a separate distribution per user for personalization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Path-based cache behaviors let static paths be cached while API paths bypass or minimize caching.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One cache behavior with a 24-hour TTL for…: Caching personalized responses for 24 hours is incorrect.
• Disable caching for the entire…: Disabling caching loses static benefits.
• Use a separate distribution per user for…: A distribution per user is impractical.

Key takeaway: Use path-based cache behaviors for mixed content.

stem: Instances in a private subnet cannot reach the internet. A NAT gateway exists. Which TWO items should be checked? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The instances use an encrypted EBS root volume
The private route table has 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway
The VPC has a private hosted zone in Route 53
The instances have Elastic IP addresses attached
The NAT gateway is in a public subnet with an IGW route

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private subnets need a default route to the NAT gateway, and the NAT gateway must sit in a public subnet with an internet gateway route.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The instances use an encrypted EBS root volume: Volume encryption is unrelated.
• The VPC has a private hosted zone in Route 53: Private hosted zones are for DNS.
• The instances have Elastic IP addresses attached: Private instances do not need Elastic IPs.

Key takeaway: Check both route tables for NAT-based internet access.

stem: On-premises servers cannot resolve names in a Route 53 private hosted zone over Direct Connect. What should be configured?

choices.text: A public hosted zone copy of every private record for the servers
A CloudFront distribution in front of the private hosted zone
A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint with on-premises DNS forwarding
A NAT gateway in the VPC for on-premises DNS queries to use

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver inbound endpoints let on-premises DNS servers forward queries to resolve private hosted zone names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A public hosted zone copy of every private…: Copying to public zones exposes internal records.
• A CloudFront distribution in front of the…: CloudFront does not serve DNS.
• A NAT gateway in the VPC for on-premises DNS…: NAT gateways do not resolve DNS.

Key takeaway: On-premises resolution of private zones → Resolver inbound endpoint.

stem: Users receive 502 errors from an ALB. Targets show as healthy, but the application sometimes closes connections unexpectedly. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: The target's keep-alive timeout is shorter than the ALB idle timeout
The target group uses more than one Availability Zone for targets
The Route 53 alias record for the ALB uses a TTL that is too short
The ALB's access logs bucket has versioning enabled on its objects

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the target closes idle connections before the ALB does, the ALB may reuse a closed connection and return 502.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The target group uses more than one…: Multiple AZs are normal.
• The Route 53 alias record for the ALB uses a…: DNS TTL does not cause 502s.
• The ALB's access logs bucket has versioning…: Log bucket settings are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Set target keep-alive longer than the ALB idle timeout.

stem: A company needs to block access to its CloudFront content from specific countries. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Route 53 latency-based routing
S3 bucket versioning settings
EC2 security group outbound rules
CloudFront geographic restrictions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront geographic restrictions allow or block viewers by country.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 latency-based routing: Latency routing directs traffic, not blocks.
• S3 bucket versioning settings: Versioning keeps object versions.
• EC2 security group outbound rules: Security groups do not apply to CloudFront viewers.

Key takeaway: Block countries at the edge with geo restrictions.

stem: A team wants to apply the same set of tags automatically to all resources created by a CloudFormation stack. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm for resources that have no tags
Add tags manually in each service console after deployment
Specify stack-level tags when creating or updating the stack
Use an S3 lifecycle rule to add tags to resources nightly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Stack-level tags propagate to supported resources created by the stack.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Create a CloudWatch alarm for resources that…: Alarms do not apply tags.
• Add tags manually in each service console…: Manual tagging is error-prone.
• Use an S3 lifecycle rule to add tags to…: Lifecycle rules do not tag resources.

Key takeaway: Propagate tags with stack-level tags.

stem: A Lambda function behind API Gateway must publish per-endpoint latency and order-value metrics to CloudWatch with an Endpoint dimension. Each log line must also keep the customer ID and request ID for later investigation. The team does not want extra synchronous API calls inside the request path. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Write each record in CloudWatch embedded metric format to standard output so CloudWatch extracts the metrics from the log events
Create one metric filter per customer ID on the function's log group so that every customer gets an individual latency metric
Call PutMetricData from the handler for every request and write the customer ID to the log as a separate plain-text log line
Add the customer ID and latency as AWS X-Ray annotations and build CloudWatch alarms directly on the resulting trace segments

explanation:
## Two ways to publish custom metrics
- **PutMetricData**: the code calls the CloudWatch API. Simple, but every call is a network round trip, costs money per request and can be throttled.
- **Embedded metric format (EMF)**: the code writes a JSON log event. A special `_aws` block lists which fields are metrics (with units) and which are dimensions. CloudWatch Logs extracts those metrics in the background.
## Why EMF suits Lambda
Lambda already ships standard output to CloudWatch Logs, so EMF adds no network call to the handler. The same log event can carry extra fields that are *not* dimensions, such as `customerId` or `requestId`. They do not become metrics (no cardinality explosion) but remain searchable with Logs Insights.
Example event: `{"_aws":{"CloudWatchMetrics":[{"Namespace":"Shop","Dimensions":[["Endpoint"]],"Metrics":[{"Name":"Latency","Unit":"Milliseconds"}]}]},"Endpoint":"/order","Latency":87,"customerId":"c-123"}`
Libraries such as Powertools for AWS Lambda generate this format for you.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Embedded metric format (correct):** the function prints a structured JSON log event with an `_aws` metadata block, and CloudWatch Logs extracts the declared metrics asynchronously. There is no extra API call in the request path, and high-cardinality fields such as the customer ID stay in the same log event for Logs Insights queries.
- ✗ **B. Metric filter per customer:** a log group supports only a limited number of metric filters (100), so one per customer does not scale, and it would create a separate high-cardinality metric for every customer.
- ✗ **C. PutMetricData per request:** it adds a synchronous network call and API cost to every invocation, can be throttled at high request rates, and splits metrics and context into separate records.
- ✗ **D. X-Ray annotations:** annotations index traces for filtering in X-Ray, but CloudWatch alarms are built on metrics, not on individual trace segments, so this does not produce the required alarmable metrics.

## Key idea
Metrics plus rich context from Lambda without extra API calls → embedded metric format in the logs, not PutMetricData or per-value metric filters.

stem: A CloudWatch alarm on an EC2 fleet's CPUUtilization uses a 1-minute period and 1 evaluation period, and it pages on single short spikes. The team wants a page only when CPU is high for most of a 5-minute window, even if one or two samples inside that window dip below the threshold. Which alarm configuration fits?

choices.text: Set evaluation periods to 5 and datapoints to alarm to 5, keeping the 1-minute period and the current CPU threshold
Set evaluation periods to 5 and datapoints to alarm to 3, keeping the 1-minute period and the current CPU threshold
Keep one evaluation period and set the alarm to treat missing data as notBreaching to suppress the brief spike alerts
Change the statistic to Maximum with a single 5-minute period and one datapoint to alarm at the current CPU threshold

explanation:
## How an alarm evaluates
A metric alarm has three settings that work together:
- **Period**: the length of one datapoint, for example 60 seconds.
- **Evaluation periods (N)**: how many of the most recent datapoints are examined.
- **Datapoints to alarm (M)**: how many of those N must breach the threshold.
## M out of N
With `Period=60`, `N=5`, `M=3` the alarm checks the last five minutes and goes to ALARM when any three minutes breach. The breaching points do not have to be consecutive.
- 1 out of 1: every spike pages.
- 5 out of 5: a single healthy minute cancels the alarm.
- 3 out of 5: short spikes are ignored and short dips do not hide a sustained problem.
The statistic also matters: `Average` smooths a period, `Maximum` reports its worst sample.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. 5 out of 5 datapoints:** every one of the five points must breach, so a single dip below the threshold resets the condition and a real sustained problem can go unreported.
- ✓ **B. 3 out of 5 datapoints (correct):** the alarm looks at the last five 1-minute points and fires when any three breach. A single spike is ignored, while sustained high CPU still alarms even if one or two samples dip.
- ✗ **C. Treat missing data as notBreaching:** this only changes how gaps in the data are evaluated. The spikes are real datapoints, not missing ones, so the alarm keeps firing on them.
- ✗ **D. Maximum over 5 minutes:** the Maximum statistic reports the highest sample in the period, so one short spike still makes the whole 5-minute datapoint breach. This makes the noise worse, not better.

## Key idea
To tolerate spikes and dips at the same time use "M out of N" datapoints to alarm; "N out of N" is too strict and Maximum amplifies spikes.

stem: Application logs in a CloudWatch Logs log group sometimes contain customer email addresses and credit card numbers. Developers must keep reading these logs for troubleshooting without seeing those values, while a small security group must still be able to view the original values. What should the CloudOps engineer configure?

choices.text: An IAM policy that denies logs:GetLogEvents and logs:FilterLogEvents on the log group for every developer role
A customer managed KMS key on the log group, granting kms:Decrypt on that key only to the members of the security group
A Logs Insights saved query that filters out lines matching card and email patterns, shared with the developer roles
A data protection policy on the log group with managed data identifiers, granting logs:Unmask only to the security group

explanation:
## Masking sensitive data in CloudWatch Logs
A **data protection policy** is attached to a log group (or set account-wide). It uses **managed data identifiers**, predefined patterns for things like email addresses, credit card numbers, AWS secret keys or national ID numbers.
- Matching text in new log events is masked, for example `card=****************`.
- The original data is kept; a principal with `logs:Unmask` can see it in the console or through `GetLogEvents` with `unmask=true`.
- The policy can also send audit findings (which identifier matched, how often) to another log group, S3 or Firehose.
## Why not just encrypt?
KMS encryption answers "who can read stored data at all". Masking answers "which parts of a record can a reader see". Here both groups need access to the logs, so only masking separates them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Deny read APIs:** this blocks developers from reading the logs entirely, which breaks the requirement that they keep troubleshooting with them.
- ✗ **B. KMS key on the log group:** encryption protects data at rest, but it never hides parts of a log event. Anyone who can read the log group sees the full values, so developers cannot be given readable logs with the sensitive fields masked.
- ✗ **C. Saved query with filters:** a saved query is only a convenience. Developers can still open the log stream or write their own query and see every sensitive value in clear text.
- ✓ **D. Data protection policy (correct):** CloudWatch Logs scans events at ingestion with managed data identifiers such as `EmailAddress` and `CreditCardNumber` and masks matches for all readers. Only principals with the `logs:Unmask` permission can view the original values.

## Key idea
Hide sensitive values while keeping logs readable → data protection policy with masking and `logs:Unmask`, not encryption or access denial.

stem: An internal reverse proxy process named haproxy on several EC2 instances is occasionally killed by the OS, but the instances keep passing status checks. Traffic is sporadic, so long periods without requests are normal. The team wants an alarm within minutes when the process is not running. What should they do?

choices.text: Configure the CloudWatch agent procstat plugin to track haproxy and alarm when the process PID count drops below 1
Stream the haproxy access log to CloudWatch Logs and alarm when the IncomingLogEvents metric drops to zero
Create alarms on StatusCheckFailed_Instance for each instance and add an EC2 reboot action when the check fails
Enable detailed monitoring on the instances and alarm when CPUUtilization falls below 1 percent for five minutes

explanation:
## What EC2 metrics can and cannot see
Default EC2 metrics come from the hypervisor: CPU, network, disk I/O and status checks. The hypervisor sees the VM, not the processes inside it.
## The procstat plugin
The unified CloudWatch agent runs inside the OS and can collect process-level data. In its config you name a process by `exe`, `pattern` or `pid_file`:
`"procstat": [{"exe": "haproxy", "measurement": ["pid_count", "cpu_usage", "memory_rss"]}]`
- `procstat_lookup_pid_count` reports how many matching processes exist.
- When the process dies the count becomes 0, and an alarm with threshold `< 1` fires on the next evaluation.
- With the instance ID appended as a dimension, create one alarm per instance to cover the fleet.
Treat missing data as breaching so the alarm also fires if the agent itself stops reporting.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. procstat plugin (correct):** the CloudWatch agent looks up processes by name or pattern and publishes metrics such as `procstat_lookup_pid_count`. An alarm on that metric below 1 fires as soon as the process disappears, independent of traffic.
- ✗ **B. IncomingLogEvents at zero:** with sporadic traffic the access log is often quiet while the proxy is healthy, so the alarm would fire constantly or have to be too slow to be useful.
- ✗ **C. Instance status check:** this check tests OS reachability and networking. A single killed process leaves the OS healthy, which is exactly why the checks keep passing.
- ✗ **D. Low CPU alarm:** idle periods are normal here, so low CPU also occurs while haproxy runs fine, and CPU from other processes can hide a dead proxy. The metric does not represent the process.

## Key idea
Watch a specific process with the CloudWatch agent's procstat plugin; hypervisor metrics and status checks cannot see individual processes.

stem: An AWS Config rule uses automatic remediation with an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook to fix noncompliant resources. Evaluations work, but every remediation execution fails with an authorization error on the API call the runbook makes. What should the CloudOps engineer do?

choices.text: Attach the permissions the runbook needs to the AWS Config service-linked role that evaluates the rule and triggers remediation
Create an IAM role that trusts ssm.amazonaws.com with the needed permissions and pass its ARN as the AutomationAssumeRole parameter
Increase the remediation retry attempts and retry interval so the runbook is re-executed until the API call eventually succeeds
Add the permissions the runbook needs to the instance profile role of every EC2 instance that is managed by Systems Manager

explanation:
## How Config remediation runs
An AWS Config rule only evaluates. When a resource is noncompliant, the remediation configuration starts an **SSM Automation** runbook such as `AWS-EnableS3BucketEncryption` or a custom one.
## Whose permissions?
Automation executes each step itself (for example `aws:executeAwsApi` calls an AWS API). It needs credentials, and remediation supplies them through the `AutomationAssumeRole` parameter:
- The role's trust policy allows `ssm.amazonaws.com` to assume it.
- Its permissions policy allows exactly what the runbook does, for example `s3:PutEncryptionConfiguration`.
- The remediation's parameter mapping sets `AutomationAssumeRole` to a static value, the role's ARN.
If the role is missing or too narrow, the rule keeps flagging the resource and the execution history shows `AccessDenied` on the step's API call.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Config service-linked role:** service-linked roles are managed by AWS and cannot be edited, and the runbook does not run with Config's credentials anyway, so its API calls would still be denied.
- ✓ **B. AutomationAssumeRole (correct):** Automation runbooks make their AWS API calls with the role passed in `AutomationAssumeRole`. That role must trust `ssm.amazonaws.com` and hold the permissions the runbook's steps need, and the remediation configuration maps its ARN into the parameter.
- ✗ **C. More retries:** an authorization error is deterministic. Retrying the same call with the same missing permission fails every time and only delays the fix.
- ✗ **D. Instance profile role:** the instance profile is used by the SSM Agent on the instance. Automation steps such as `aws:executeAwsApi` run in the Automation service, not on the instances, so they never use that role.

## Key idea
Config remediation runs as the Automation assume role you supply; fix permissions there, not in Config's own role or the instance profile.

stem: After the security team enabled server-side encryption on an SNS topic using the AWS managed key aws/sns, CloudWatch alarms that publish to the topic still enter ALARM, but no notifications arrive. The alarm history shows the action failed. Subscriptions are confirmed. What is the fix?

choices.text: Add cloudwatch.amazonaws.com to the aws/sns key policy so the CloudWatch service principal can call kms:GenerateDataKey
Recreate the alarms so their actions use the SNS topic's delivery policy instead of publishing to the topic ARN directly
Re-encrypt the topic with a customer managed KMS key whose key policy allows cloudwatch.amazonaws.com to use the key
Delete and re-create the email subscriptions so each subscriber confirms the new encrypted delivery path of the topic

explanation:
## Encrypted SNS topics
With server-side encryption, SNS encrypts each message with a data key from AWS KMS. The **publisher** therefore needs KMS permissions on the topic's key, not only `sns:Publish`.
## AWS managed vs customer managed keys
- **AWS managed key** (`alias/aws/sns`): free and automatic, but its key policy is fixed. It only allows principals in your account that use SNS on their own behalf.
- **Customer managed key**: you write the key policy, so you can allow AWS service principals.
Key policy statement for CloudWatch alarms:
`{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"cloudwatch.amazonaws.com"},"Action":["kms:Decrypt","kms:GenerateDataKey*"],"Resource":"*"}`
The same pattern applies to EventBridge, S3 event notifications and other services that publish to encrypted topics.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Edit the aws/sns key policy:** AWS managed key policies are owned by AWS and cannot be modified, so this grant cannot be made.
- ✗ **B. Use the delivery policy:** a delivery policy controls retries for HTTP/S endpoints. Alarms always publish to a topic ARN, and the KMS permission problem remains.
- ✓ **C. Customer managed key (correct):** CloudWatch must be allowed to call `kms:GenerateDataKey*` and `kms:Decrypt` to publish to an encrypted topic. The key policy of an AWS managed key cannot be changed, so the topic needs a customer managed key whose policy grants these actions to `cloudwatch.amazonaws.com`.
- ✗ **D. Re-create subscriptions:** the failure happens when CloudWatch publishes to the topic, before any delivery to subscribers. Confirmed subscriptions are not the problem and re-confirming changes nothing.

## Key idea
Services that publish to encrypted SNS topics (such as CloudWatch alarms) need a customer managed key they are allowed to use; aws/sns cannot be shared with them.

stem: New EC2 instances in a private subnet do not appear as managed nodes in Systems Manager, so Run Command and Session Manager cannot reach them. The AMI includes a current SSM Agent, and the account does not use Default Host Management Configuration. Which TWO causes should the engineer check? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The security group does not allow inbound TCP 443 from the Systems Manager service endpoints
The instances were launched without an EC2 key pair, so the agent cannot sign its registration
The security group does not allow inbound TCP 22 from the Systems Manager service IP ranges
The subnet has no NAT gateway route and no interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages
The instance profile does not include the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy

explanation:
## How a node becomes "managed"
The SSM Agent on the instance calls the Systems Manager service outbound over HTTPS (port 443). Three things must be true:
- **Agent** installed and running (true here).
- **Credentials**: normally an instance profile role with the managed policy `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`. (Default Host Management Configuration can supply them instead, but it is not enabled here.)
- **Network path** to the endpoints `ssm.<region>.amazonaws.com`, `ssmmessages...` and `ec2messages...`.
## Private subnets
A private subnet has no internet gateway route. The path must come from:
- a NAT gateway route `0.0.0.0/0 → nat-...`, or
- interface VPC endpoints for the three services, with private DNS enabled and a security group on the endpoints allowing 443 from the instances.
Nothing needs to reach the instance inbound, which is why Session Manager works without open ports.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Inbound HTTPS rule:** the connection is initiated outbound by the agent; security groups are stateful, so return traffic is allowed without any inbound rule.
- ✗ **B. Missing key pair:** key pairs are only for SSH or RDP logins. The agent authenticates with the instance profile's IAM credentials, not a key pair.
- ✗ **C. Inbound SSH rule:** Systems Manager does not use SSH. The agent opens outbound connections, so no inbound port is needed at all.
- ✓ **D. Outbound path from the private subnet (correct):** the agent must reach the service endpoints over outbound HTTPS, through a NAT gateway or through interface VPC endpoints for `ssm`, `ssmmessages` and `ec2messages`.
- ✓ **E. Instance profile permissions (correct):** the SSM Agent registers with Systems Manager using the instance profile credentials, which need `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` when Default Host Management Configuration is not used.

## Key idea
A node becomes managed when the agent has IAM permissions and an outbound path to the SSM endpoints; inbound ports and key pairs play no role.

stem: During a disaster recovery drill, EBS volumes for a database are created from snapshots. For the first hour the database shows extremely high read latency, then performance becomes normal. The runbook requires full volume performance as soon as the restored instances start. What should the team do?

choices.text: Register the snapshots as an AMI and launch the database instances from it so the volumes are created during instance launch
Enable EBS fast snapshot restore on the snapshots in the Availability Zones where the recovery volumes will be created
Restore the volumes as io2 with much higher provisioned IOPS than production so reads have enough headroom right away
Choose a larger instance type with more dedicated EBS bandwidth so reads from the new volumes are not limited by the instance

explanation:
## How a volume is restored from a snapshot
Snapshots live in Amazon S3. When you create an EBS volume from one, the volume is usable at once, but its blocks are pulled from S3 **the first time they are read**. That first access can be much slower than normal, which is called volume initialization.
## Ways to avoid the penalty
- **Fast snapshot restore (FSR)**: enabled per snapshot and per Availability Zone. Volumes created from it in those AZs are fully initialized at creation. Billed per snapshot-AZ hour, so enable it before drills or for critical DR snapshots.
- **Pre-warm by reading everything**: run `fio` or `dd` over the whole device after restore. It works without extra cost but takes time proportional to the volume size.
Example: a 2 TiB database volume restored normally might take hours to warm under load; with FSR on `snap-0abc` in `us-east-1a`, the volume created in `us-east-1a` performs fully from its first read.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Launch from an AMI:** an AMI is backed by the same EBS snapshots, so its volumes are also initialized lazily and show the same first-read latency.
- ✓ **B. Fast snapshot restore (correct):** volumes created from a snapshot normally load blocks lazily from Amazon S3 on first access. With fast snapshot restore enabled for a snapshot in an AZ, volumes created there are fully initialized at creation and deliver full performance immediately.
- ✗ **C. Higher provisioned IOPS:** the delay comes from fetching each block from S3 on first read, not from the IOPS limit. Extra IOPS do not remove the first-read penalty.
- ✗ **D. Larger instance type:** the instance was not the bottleneck; performance becomes normal later on the same instance once blocks are loaded, which points to volume initialization.

## Key idea
Slow first reads on restored volumes come from lazy loading; fast snapshot restore (or pre-reading every block) removes it, more IOPS or bigger instances do not.

stem: A CPU-bound image-processing Lambda function is configured with 512 MB of memory and takes about 8 seconds per invocation. CloudWatch shows it uses only 180 MB of memory, so a teammate proposes reducing memory to save cost. What should the CloudOps engineer recommend?

choices.text: Test higher memory settings, because Lambda assigns CPU in proportion to memory and shorter runs can cost less
Configure provisioned concurrency for the function, because it gives each execution environment dedicated CPU
Increase the function timeout, because the 8-second duration shows the function is close to hitting its limit
Reduce the memory to 256 MB, because billed cost scales with configured memory and the extra memory is unused

explanation:
## Memory is the only compute knob in Lambda
You set memory from 128 MB to 10,240 MB. CPU and network bandwidth are assigned in proportion:
- About 1,769 MB equals one vCPU.
- 10,240 MB gives up to 6 vCPUs (useful only if the code is multithreaded).
## Cost is memory x time
Lambda bills GB-seconds. Example for this function:
- 512 MB x 8 s = 4 GB-s
- 1,536 MB x 2.5 s = 3.75 GB-s: faster **and** slightly cheaper.
- 256 MB x 16 s = 4 GB-s: same cost, twice as slow.
## How to choose
Run the function at several memory sizes and compare duration and cost. AWS Lambda Power Tuning automates this, and AWS Compute Optimizer gives memory recommendations from real invocations. The "Max Memory Used" value in the logs only tells you the floor, not the best setting.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Raise memory to get CPU (correct):** Lambda allocates CPU power proportionally to the memory setting (about one full vCPU at 1,769 MB, up to 6 vCPUs at 10,240 MB). A CPU-bound function often finishes several times faster with more memory, and because cost is memory x duration, the total can stay the same or drop.
- ✗ **B. Provisioned concurrency:** it keeps environments initialized to avoid cold starts. It does not give an invocation more CPU than its memory setting allows.
- ✗ **C. Longer timeout:** nothing indicates timeouts are occurring, and a longer limit does not make the code run faster.
- ✗ **D. Reduce to 256 MB:** it halves the CPU share too, so a CPU-bound function runs roughly twice as long. Cost per invocation barely changes while latency gets worse.

## Key idea
For CPU-bound Lambda functions memory is the CPU dial; tune it by measuring duration and cost, not by memory used.

stem: A database on an m5.large instance uses an io2 volume provisioned for 40,000 IOPS, but under load it never gets close. CloudWatch shows the instance's EBSIOBalance% draining to zero and volume IOPS then settling far below the provisioned value. What should the CloudOps engineer do?

choices.text: Modify the io2 volume to raise its provisioned IOPS further so that it can push more operations through the same instance
Turn on the EBS-optimized attribute for the instance so that storage traffic gets its own dedicated network bandwidth
Move to an instance type whose EBS-optimized IOPS and bandwidth limits meet or exceed the volume's provisioned performance
Stripe two io2 volumes in RAID 0 on the same instance so that the operating system can spread its I/O across both volumes

explanation:
## Two limits on every EBS I/O
Each I/O must fit within both:
- the **volume** limit (for example provisioned io2 IOPS), and
- the **instance** EBS limit, which depends on instance type and size.
## Burst EBS performance on smaller instances
Many smaller sizes list EBS performance as "up to" a value. They have a lower **baseline** and can burst above it for a limited time (around 30 minutes per day) using credits. CloudWatch exposes the credits as `EBSIOBalance%` (IOPS) and `EBSByteBalance%` (throughput).
Example: the volume allows 40,000 IOPS, but a small instance's baseline is a few thousand IOPS. When `EBSIOBalance%` reaches 0 the volume metrics flatten at the instance baseline.
## What to do
Compare the instance type's documented EBS baseline IOPS and throughput with the volume's needs and pick a size or family that meets them in sustained operation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Raise volume IOPS:** the volume is already provisioned above what the instance can deliver. More volume IOPS cannot pass through an instance-level cap.
- ✗ **B. Enable EBS-optimized:** current-generation types like m5 are EBS-optimized by default. The attribute is already in effect, and the limit being hit is the size of that dedicated bandwidth.
- ✓ **C. Bigger EBS limit on the instance (correct):** every instance type has its own maximum EBS IOPS and throughput. Smaller sizes can burst above a low baseline only while their EBS I/O credits (`EBSIOBalance%`) last. Once the balance is empty the instance, not the volume, caps performance, so the fix is an instance type with higher sustained EBS limits.
- ✗ **D. RAID 0 across two volumes:** striping helps when a single volume is the limit. Both volumes share the same instance EBS limit, so the total stays capped.

## Key idea
EBS performance is the lower of the volume's and the instance's limits; a draining EBSIOBalance% means resize the instance, not the volume.

stem: A provisioned-capacity DynamoDB table uses event_date as its partition key. Writes for the current day are throttled even though the table's consumed WCU is far below provisioned WCU. The team wants to confirm the cause and fix it for the long term. Which TWO actions should they take? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Add a global secondary index keyed on event_date so the writes for the current day are divided between table and index
Put DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table so that the write traffic for the current day is absorbed
Double the table's provisioned WCU so that each partition receives a larger share of the total write capacity
Redesign the key with a higher-cardinality partition key or add a calculated suffix to spread writes across partitions
Enable CloudWatch Contributor Insights for DynamoDB on the table to identify the most throttled partition keys

explanation:
## Partitions and their limits
DynamoDB stores items in partitions chosen by hashing the partition key. Each partition supports up to **3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU**. Adaptive capacity shifts unused capacity toward busy partitions, but it cannot fully absorb traffic that is concentrated on one partition key value.
## The hot-key pattern
With `event_date` as the key, every write of the day has the same key, so all writes land on one partition. The table total looks fine, yet requests are throttled.
## Diagnose and fix
- **Contributor Insights for DynamoDB**: ranks keys by traffic and by throttled requests.
- **Write sharding**: append a random or calculated suffix, `event_date#0` ... `event_date#9`, and query all suffixes when reading a day.
- **Better key**: use a high-cardinality attribute such as `device_id` and keep the date as the sort key.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. GSI on event_date:** the index has the same hot key, and writes to the table must also be written to the index. A throttled GSI adds back-pressure instead of relieving it.
- ✗ **B. Add DAX:** DAX caches reads. Writes go through DAX to the table (write-through), so the hot-partition writes still hit the same partition.
- ✗ **C. Double provisioned WCU:** a single partition still cannot exceed about 1,000 WCU. When all writes target one key, raising the table total leaves that partition's limit unchanged.
- ✓ **D. Higher-cardinality key or write sharding (correct):** a key with more distinct values, or a suffix such as `2026-09-29#7`, spreads the writes across many partitions and removes the hot key.
- ✓ **E. Contributor Insights for DynamoDB (correct):** it ranks the most accessed and most throttled partition keys, confirming that one date value receives nearly all of the day's writes.

## Key idea
Throttling with spare table capacity means a hot partition key; find it with Contributor Insights and fix the key design, not the capacity.

stem: Instances in an Auto Scaling group need about 12 minutes after launch to load application data before they can serve traffic. Traffic spikes are unpredictable. The team wants new capacity in service within about a minute of a scale-out, while paying as little as possible for pre-initialized capacity that is waiting. Which solution fits best?

choices.text: Add a warm pool to the Auto Scaling group with the pool state set to Stopped and use a lifecycle hook to initialize instances
Raise the group's minimum capacity to cover the largest expected spike so that initialized instances are always in service
Enable predictive scaling on the group in forecast-and-scale mode so that instances are launched ahead of each spike
Add a warm pool to the Auto Scaling group with the pool state set to Running so initialized instances can join immediately

explanation:
## What a warm pool is
A **warm pool** is a set of pre-initialized EC2 instances kept next to an Auto Scaling group. On scale-out, the group takes instances from the warm pool instead of launching fresh ones, skipping the slow boot and application setup.
## Pool states and cost
- **Running**: instances run but receive no traffic. Fastest, full compute cost.
- **Stopped**: instances are stopped after initialization. You pay only for storage (EBS) and Elastic IPs. Starting takes seconds to a minute.
- **Hibernated**: memory is saved to EBS, useful when in-memory state is expensive to rebuild.
## How initialization works
A lifecycle hook on the warm pool launch runs your setup (download data, warm caches), then completes the hook and the instance moves to its pool state. Example: `MinSize=4`, warm pool `MinSize=6`, state `Stopped`; a spike moves up to six ready instances into service within about a minute.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Warm pool in Stopped state (correct):** instances are launched, fully initialized once by a lifecycle hook, then stopped. While stopped you pay only for EBS volumes and attached Elastic IPs; on scale-out they start in seconds with the application data already loaded.
- ✗ **B. Higher minimum capacity:** the extra instances run and serve traffic all the time, costing full price around the clock just to cover rare spikes.
- ✗ **C. Predictive scaling:** it forecasts from recurring daily or weekly patterns. Unpredictable spikes have no pattern to learn, so instances would still launch late.
- ✗ **D. Warm pool in Running state:** it gives the fastest join, but you pay full instance-hours for every waiting instance, which is not the lowest cost for idle capacity.

## Key idea
Long boot plus unpredictable spikes → warm pool; Stopped state keeps pre-initialized capacity cheap, Running state is faster but pays for compute.

stem: An API fleet behind an ALB is limited by calls to a downstream service, not by CPU. Load tests show each instance handles about 500 requests per minute before latency rises, while CPU stays under 30%. A CPU-based target tracking policy therefore never scales out. Which policy fits best?

choices.text: Step scaling on the NetworkIn metric of the group, adding instances as inbound bytes cross set thresholds
Target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget with a target value somewhat below 500 requests per target
Scheduled scaling that adds instances during business hours and removes them in the evening each weekday
Target tracking on average CPUUtilization with the target value lowered from 50 percent to 20 percent

explanation:
## Choosing a scaling metric
Target tracking keeps one metric near a target value. It only works well when the metric grows in proportion to load **and** reflects what actually saturates the instance.
## Request-bound workloads
Some services spend their time waiting on a database or downstream API. Their CPU stays low while latency climbs, so CPU never tells Auto Scaling that more capacity is needed.
## ALBRequestCountPerTarget
- Predefined metric for EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking, tied to one ALB target group.
- Value = requests to the target group per minute divided by healthy targets.
- Example: capacity found in testing is 500 per instance; set the target to about 400 to keep headroom. At 4,000 requests per minute the group aims for 10 instances.
Other load-proportional choices are SQS backlog per instance for queue workers or a custom metric such as active connections.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Step scaling on NetworkIn:** inbound bytes depend on request size, not on request count, and step thresholds must be tuned by hand. It tracks the real limit poorly.
- ✓ **B. ALBRequestCountPerTarget (correct):** this predefined metric divides the target group's request count by the number of healthy targets, which is exactly the per-instance limit found in testing. Target tracking adds instances when the per-target count rises toward the target and removes them when it falls.
- ✗ **C. Scheduled scaling:** it follows the clock, not demand, so load outside the expected pattern still overloads the fleet.
- ✗ **D. Lower CPU target:** CPU is only loosely related to this workload's real bottleneck, so a 20% target scales at the wrong times, too early at some loads and too late at others.

## Key idea
Scale on the metric that represents the bottleneck; for request-bound web fleets that is requests per target, not CPU.

stem: An ECS service on EC2 container instances uses service auto scaling. During peaks the desired task count rises, but new tasks stay unplaced with events reporting insufficient memory. The cluster's Auto Scaling group scales only on average instance CPU, which stays low. What should the CloudOps engineer do?

choices.text: Change the service's task placement strategy to binpack on memory so that tasks fill the existing instances more tightly
Add a target tracking policy on the cluster's CPUReservation metric so the Auto Scaling group grows as CPU is reserved
Raise the maximum task count in the service auto scaling policy so the service can request more tasks during the peaks
Create an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling and use it in the service's capacity provider strategy

explanation:
## Two layers of scaling in ECS on EC2
- **Service auto scaling** changes how many **tasks** a service wants (Application Auto Scaling).
- **Cluster capacity** is the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. If tasks need more CPU or memory than free capacity, they cannot be placed.
Scaling the group on instance CPU utilization ignores memory and ignores tasks that are still waiting.
## Capacity providers with managed scaling
An **Auto Scaling group capacity provider** links the group to the cluster. With managed scaling on, ECS publishes `CapacityProviderReservation` (capacity needed / capacity available x 100) and creates a target tracking policy on it.
- Target 100 means "no spare instances"; a lower target such as 90 keeps headroom.
- Waiting tasks raise the metric above target, so instances launch until the tasks fit.
The service uses it through `capacityProviderStrategy: [{"capacityProvider": "cp-web", "weight": 1}]`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Binpack on memory:** binpacking only changes where tasks go on existing instances. When memory across the cluster is already insufficient, no placement strategy can create room.
- ✗ **B. Scale on CPUReservation:** the tasks are blocked by memory, not CPU. Reserved CPU can stay low while memory is exhausted, so the group still does not grow.
- ✗ **C. Raise maximum task count:** the service already asks for more tasks; the problem is where to run them. A higher ceiling just adds more unplaced tasks.
- ✓ **D. Capacity provider with managed scaling (correct):** ECS computes the `CapacityProviderReservation` metric from the CPU and memory that tasks need, including tasks waiting for placement, and scales the Auto Scaling group to fit them. Unplaced tasks then trigger new instances automatically.

## Key idea
For ECS on EC2, let a capacity provider with managed scaling grow the instances from task needs; instance CPU or a single reservation metric misses memory-bound shortfalls.

stem: A latency-sensitive Lambda function behind API Gateway has multi-second cold starts because of heavy initialization. Every weekday traffic jumps sharply at 08:00 and stays high until 18:00, and is low at night. The team wants requests during business hours to avoid initialization delays without paying for idle warm capacity at night. What should they configure?

choices.text: Reserved concurrency on the function, adjusted by an EventBridge Scheduler job before 08:00 and after 18:00 every weekday
An EventBridge rule that invokes the function every five minutes during business hours to keep its execution environments warm
Provisioned concurrency on a function alias, adjusted by Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions before 08:00 and after 18:00
A larger memory setting and a longer timeout during business hours, applied and reverted by an EventBridge Scheduler job

explanation:
## Cold starts
When Lambda needs a new execution environment it downloads the code and runs the initialization code (imports, SDK clients, model loading) before the handler. That delay is the cold start.
## Reserved vs provisioned concurrency
- **Reserved concurrency**: guarantees and limits the number of concurrent executions a function can use. No environment is created in advance.
- **Provisioned concurrency**: Lambda creates and initializes N environments ahead of time on a published version or alias. Requests up to N run without init delay. You pay per hour while it is configured.
## Scheduling it
Provisioned concurrency is a scalable target in Application Auto Scaling (`lambda:function:ProvisionedConcurrency`). Example:
- `cron(45 7 ? * MON-FRI *)`: set min capacity to 200.
- `cron(0 18 ? * MON-FRI *)`: set it back to a small night-time value.
A target tracking policy on utilization can be added for traffic above the scheduled level.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reserved concurrency:** it reserves and caps how many concurrent executions the function may use, but it does not pre-initialize any environment, so cold starts remain.
- ✗ **B. Ping every five minutes:** a ping keeps roughly one environment warm. A sharp surge needs many concurrent environments, and each new one still pays the initialization cost.
- ✓ **C. Scheduled provisioned concurrency (correct):** provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of execution environments initialized before requests arrive. Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions on the alias raise it just before 08:00 and lower it after 18:00, so you pay for warm environments only during business hours.
- ✗ **D. Bigger memory and timeout:** more memory can shorten initialization somewhat, but new environments still initialize on first request, and a timeout change has no effect on startup.

## Key idea
Pre-initialized capacity on a schedule → provisioned concurrency with scheduled scaling; reserved concurrency only caps, and pings only keep one environment warm.

stem: A fault-tolerant batch fleet runs on Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group. It currently uses one instance type with the lowest-price allocation strategy and loses many instances at once during interruptions. Which TWO changes improve availability of Spot capacity? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Keep the single instance type but set a low maximum Spot price to avoid the most contested capacity
Restrict the group to one Availability Zone so that all Spot requests draw from the same capacity pool
Allow many suitable instance types and use the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy
Switch the allocation strategy to lowest-price and set the number of pools to use for Spot to only one
Enable Capacity Rebalancing so replacements launch when instances receive a rebalance recommendation

explanation:
## Spot capacity pools
A **Spot capacity pool** is one instance type in one Availability Zone. AWS reclaims Spot capacity pool by pool. A fleet in a single pool is interrupted all at once; a fleet spread over many pools loses only a slice.
## Allocation strategies in a mixed instances policy
- `lowest-price`: fills the cheapest pools; highest interruption risk.
- `capacity-optimized`: pools with the most available capacity.
- `price-capacity-optimized` (recommended): deep pools that are also low priced.
Diversify with a list of types or with attribute-based selection, for example "4-8 vCPU, 16-32 GiB, current generation".
## Capacity Rebalancing
EC2 sends a **rebalance recommendation** when an instance is at elevated risk, often before the two-minute interruption notice. With Capacity Rebalancing on, the group launches a replacement first, then terminates the at-risk instance after the new one is running.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Low maximum price:** Spot prices move gradually with long-term supply and demand, and interruptions are mainly driven by capacity. A low max price can also make requests fail or be interrupted more, while one type still means one pool.
- ✗ **B. Single Availability Zone:** fewer AZs means fewer capacity pools. When that one pool is reclaimed the whole fleet is hit at once, the opposite of the goal.
- ✓ **C. Diversify with price-capacity-optimized (correct):** many instance types across several AZs give many Spot capacity pools, and this strategy picks pools with deep capacity at a low price.
- ✗ **D. Lowest-price from one pool:** this concentrates the whole fleet in the cheapest pool, which is often the most contested, so one reclaim event interrupts most instances.
- ✓ **E. Capacity Rebalancing (correct):** when an instance receives a rebalance recommendation, the group launches a replacement first, often before the two-minute interruption notice arrives.

## Key idea
Spot availability comes from many capacity pools plus proactive replacement; price-capacity-optimized with instance diversity and Capacity Rebalancing beats cheapest-single-pool.

stem: An application behind an ALB runs in three Availability Zones. Instances in one AZ start returning slow, partial responses while still passing health checks, a gray failure. The team wants to move traffic away from that AZ for the load balancer within minutes, without changing infrastructure, and move it back easily later. What should they do?

choices.text: Change the Route 53 record to a failover policy that points to a standby stack running in another AWS Region
Start a zonal shift in Amazon Application Recovery Controller for the load balancer away from the impaired AZ
Tighten the target group health check thresholds so the ALB marks the slow instances in that zone as unhealthy
Turn off cross-zone load balancing on the target group so that the other zones no longer send traffic to that zone

explanation:
## Gray failures
A **gray failure** is partial: instances are up and health checks pass, yet real requests are slow or fail. Automatic health checks often cannot detect it, so operators need a quick manual lever.
## Zonal shift
Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) offers **zonal shift** for supported resources, including Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers.
- You pick the resource, the AZ to move away from, and an expiry (up to several days, extendable).
- The load balancer stops routing traffic to that AZ; the remaining AZs take the load, so plan capacity for losing one AZ.
- Cancelling or letting the shift expire returns traffic to the AZ.
**Zonal autoshift** lets AWS start such a shift automatically when it detects an AZ impairment, with regular practice runs to prove that the application can handle it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cross-Region DNS failover:** moving the whole application to another Region is far bigger than needed for one bad AZ, depends on a standby stack, and the two healthy AZs would be abandoned.
- ✓ **B. Zonal shift (correct):** Application Recovery Controller temporarily moves traffic for a supported resource such as an ALB away from one Availability Zone. It needs no infrastructure change, takes effect within minutes, expires after the duration you set, and can be cancelled to bring the AZ back.
- ✗ **C. Stricter health checks:** in a gray failure the health check path keeps passing. Guessing thresholds during an incident is slow, can mark healthy targets unhealthy, and is not quickly reversible.
- ✗ **D. Disable cross-zone load balancing:** without cross-zone, each load balancer node sends only to targets in its own zone, so the impaired zone's node would send all its share to the slow instances. It does not remove the zone from service.

## Key idea
One impaired AZ behind a load balancer → zonal shift; it is fast, temporary and reversible, unlike health check tuning or Regional failover.

stem: A company uses an Aurora global database with its primary cluster in us-east-1 and a secondary cluster in eu-west-1. For a planned quarterly exercise, the team must make eu-west-1 the primary with no data loss and keep the global database replication topology intact. Which action fits?

choices.text: Restore a cross-Region snapshot copy in eu-west-1 and point applications to it
Run a global database failover with the allow data loss option selected for it
Detach the eu-west-1 cluster from the global database and then promote it alone
Run a global database switchover to promote the eu-west-1 cluster to primary

explanation:
## Aurora global database
One **primary** cluster in a Region accepts writes; up to several **secondary** clusters in other Regions receive storage-level replication, typically with under one second of lag.
## Two ways to change the primary
- **Switchover** (formerly "managed planned failover"): for healthy clusters and planned events such as Region rotation or DR drills. Aurora stops writes, waits until the secondary has caught up, then swaps roles. RPO is 0 and the replication topology is preserved.
- **Failover**: for when the primary Region is impaired. The chosen secondary is promoted without waiting, so a small amount of recent data may be lost (RPO is the replication lag), in exchange for the fastest recovery.
- **Detach and promote**: turns a secondary into an independent cluster; replication stops for it.
After either role change, applications must use the new writer endpoint, or a global writer endpoint that follows the primary.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Restore a snapshot copy:** a snapshot is a point-in-time copy, so every change after it is lost, and restoring a new cluster takes much longer than a role change.
- ✗ **B. Failover with data loss allowed:** it is meant for an unplanned Regional outage. It promotes the secondary without waiting for synchronization, so recent transactions can be lost, which the planned exercise must avoid.
- ✗ **C. Detach and promote:** removing the secondary from the global database breaks replication. The promoted cluster stands alone and the global topology must be rebuilt afterward.
- ✓ **D. Switchover (correct):** designed for planned operations on a healthy global database. Aurora waits until the chosen secondary is fully synchronized before changing roles, so no committed data is lost (RPO 0), and the old primary becomes a secondary in the same global topology.

## Key idea
Planned Region rotation with RPO 0 → switchover; failover is for outages and may lose data, detaching breaks the topology.

stem: A primary site depends on three independently monitored endpoints: web, API, and payments. Route 53 failover should send users to a secondary site only when at least two of the three endpoints are unhealthy, not when a single one fails. How should the health check for the primary failover record be built?

choices.text: Create a calculated health check with the three endpoint checks as children that is healthy when at least two are healthy
Associate all three endpoint health checks directly with the primary failover record so Route 53 counts the failures
Replace the failover records with multivalue answer records that list each of the three endpoints with its own check
Enable Evaluate Target Health on the primary record so Route 53 averages the health of the three endpoints behind it

explanation:
## Route 53 health check types
- **Endpoint** checks call an IP or domain name over HTTP, HTTPS or TCP.
- **CloudWatch alarm** checks follow the state of an alarm.
- **Calculated** checks monitor other health checks (children).
## Calculated health checks
You choose up to 256 child checks and a rule:
- healthy if **all** children are healthy,
- healthy if **at least one** is healthy, or
- healthy if **at least N** are healthy.
Example: children `hc-web`, `hc-api`, `hc-pay`, rule "at least 2 healthy". One failure leaves the parent healthy; a second failure makes it unhealthy.
## Using it with failover routing
Each record can reference one health check. Attach the calculated check to the `PRIMARY` failover record. When the parent is unhealthy, Route 53 answers with the `SECONDARY` record. The children do not need to be associated with any record.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Calculated health check (correct):** it combines the status of child health checks with a rule such as "healthy if at least 2 of 3 children are healthy". Associating it with the primary record makes failover happen only when two or more endpoints are down.
- ✗ **B. Three checks on one record:** a Route 53 record accepts only one health check ID, so there is no built-in counting across several checks attached to one record.
- ✗ **C. Multivalue answer records:** they return several healthy IP addresses for load spreading. They do not model primary/secondary sites or a two-of-three failure rule.
- ✗ **D. Evaluate Target Health:** it applies to alias records and inherits the health of the alias target, such as a load balancer. It cannot combine three separate endpoints with a threshold.

## Key idea
To fail over on a combination of conditions use a calculated health check with a child threshold; a record can carry only one health check.

stem: A company keeps month-end EBS snapshots for seven years for compliance. They are almost never restored, and a restore that takes up to three days is acceptable. Daily snapshots are kept for only 14 days. How can the company reduce storage cost for the month-end snapshots the most?

choices.text: Export the month-end snapshots to an S3 bucket and add a lifecycle rule that moves them to Glacier Deep Archive
Keep the month-end snapshots in the standard tier and delete all earlier snapshots so that only changes are stored
Create an AMI from each month-end snapshot and deregister it so that only the underlying snapshot storage remains
Move the month-end snapshots to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier with a Data Lifecycle Manager archiving rule

explanation:
## Snapshot tiers
- **Standard**: incremental snapshots, instant restore, higher price per GB-month.
- **Archive**: a full snapshot copy in a cheaper tier. Minimum retention 90 days (deleting earlier is charged for 90 days), restore to standard takes up to 72 hours before a volume can be created.
## When archive pays off
Incremental standard snapshots are cheap when there are many close copies. For one snapshot per month kept for years, each archived copy is full but billed at a much lower rate, which usually wins.
Example: a 500 GiB month-end snapshot kept for 84 months, restored perhaps once for an audit with a few days' notice.
## Automating it
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies can create snapshots on a schedule and include an **archiving rule** for a monthly schedule, so snapshots that leave the standard tier move to the archive tier and are kept there for 7 years. Restores use `RestoreSnapshotTier`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Export to S3 Glacier:** EBS snapshots are stored by AWS in a service-managed location. There is no feature to export a snapshot as objects into your own bucket for S3 lifecycle rules.
- ✗ **B. Standard tier only:** standard snapshots are incremental, but each one still references the blocks it needs, so deleting older ones saves little. The seven-year data stays at the standard storage price.
- ✗ **C. AMI then deregister:** an AMI adds no storage of its own; deregistering it leaves the same snapshots in the standard tier at the same price.
- ✓ **D. EBS Snapshots Archive (correct):** an archived snapshot is stored as a full copy in a low-cost tier (up to about 75% cheaper than standard). It suits snapshots kept 90 days or longer and rarely restored; restoring takes up to 72 hours, which fits the three-day allowance. Data Lifecycle Manager can archive snapshots automatically.

## Key idea
Long-term, rarely restored EBS snapshots → Snapshots Archive tier; it is full-copy, cheaper, 90-day minimum, restore up to 72 hours.

stem: A team adds a Cross-Region Replication rule to an existing versioned S3 bucket holding 40 million objects. New uploads replicate, but the objects that existed before the rule do not. The copies must keep their version IDs and metadata, and the team needs a completion report. What should the engineer do?
